# Gyral 0.3.8: complete documentation

> Gyral is a small framework for web components: intents in, a pure update, a pure view out. Server rendering, forms, routing and testing built in.

Generated from https://gyral.dev. Each section below is one page; its source URL follows its title.

---

# Gyral documentation

> Learn Gyral, the Model-View-Intent framework for web components: guides, concepts and reference.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/

Gyral builds web components from three pure parts. **Intent** turns platform events into typed
messages, **update** turns messages into new state, and **view** turns state into HTML. Side
effects such as HTTP, routing and timers are returned from update as data, and drivers carry them
out at the edges of your app.

New here? Start with [Getting started](https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/). It takes about ten minutes and
ends with a working, tested component. Writing code with an agent? Connect it to Gyral's MCP
server first: [Use Gyral with coding agents](https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/).

The guides build on each other, but each one stands alone. The [API reference](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/) is
generated from the published type declarations, so it always matches the code.

---

# Getting started

> Install Gyral, write your first Model-View-Intent component, use it in a page, and test it without a browser.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/

In this guide you'll create a Gyral app, write a counter component, put it on a page, and test
it. You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org) 24 or later and a package manager. The examples use
npm; pnpm and yarn work the same way.

## Create a project

The quickest start is `create-gyral`. It sets up a Vite project with Gyral, TypeScript and a
first test:

```sh
npm create gyral@latest my-app -- --template ssr
cd my-app
npm install
npm run dev
```

There are two templates:

- **`basic`**: a client-rendered app. The page loads and your components render in the
  browser. It builds [client-only](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/#client-only-builds), without
  hydration code; remove `clientOnly: true` from `vite.config.ts` before you render any page
  on a server.
- **`ssr`**: the same component rendered on the server first, so the page works before any
  JavaScript loads, then [hydrated](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/) in place.

Leave out `--template` and it asks you which one you want.

### Or set it up by hand

Gyral works with any bundler. To add it to a [Vite](https://vite.dev) project yourself:

```sh
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template vanilla-ts
cd my-app
npm install @gyral/core
```

`@gyral/core` is the whole runtime: Gyral renders with its own view layer and has no runtime
dependencies.

Then add Gyral's Vite plugins, `gyral()`. They add the template compiler to `vite build`: every
template is checked and precompiled, so a mistake fails the build with a code frame and the
bundle doesn't carry the code that prepares templates at runtime:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { gyral } from '@gyral/core/vite';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [gyral()],
});
```

List plugins of your own beside it: `plugins: [gyral(), mine()]`.

To see the same checks in your editor, add the ESLint config from `@gyral/core/eslint` (see
[Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#checked-before-it-runs)). Optionally, `npm install -D parse5` lets the
compiler check markup against a full HTML parser too.

## Write a component

A component is a custom element defined from four parts: its initial state, the intents it
understands, how each message changes the state, and how the state looks.

```ts
// src/counter.ts
import { define, html } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly count: number;
}

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Increment' } | { readonly _tag: 'Decrement' };

export const Counter = define<State, Msg>()('my-counter', {
  init: () => ({ count: 0 }),
  intent: {
    Increment: () => ({ _tag: 'Increment' }),
    Decrement: () => ({ _tag: 'Decrement' }),
  },
  update: {
    Increment: (s) => ({ count: s.count + 1 }),
    Decrement: (s) => ({ count: s.count - 1 }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Decrement}>Decrement</button>
    <output aria-live="polite">${s.count}</output>
    <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Increment}>Increment</button>
  `,
});
```

Read it from the bottom up:

- **The view** is an `html` template. It doesn't attach event handlers. Instead it _names_ an
  intent on each button with `data-intent`. `i` is typed from your messages, so a misspelt
  `i.Incremnt` is a compile error.
- **Intent** says how a platform event becomes a message. A click on a button carrying
  `data-intent=${i.Increment}` runs the `Increment` parser, which returns
  `{ _tag: 'Increment' }`. A parser can also read the event's value, form data or key, and
  return `undefined` to decline it.
- **Update** has one reducer per message, and TypeScript checks you have one for every message.
  A reducer returns the next state and never changes the old one.
- **Init** gives the state the component starts with.

## Use it in a page

`define()` registers the element, so importing the module is enough. Replace the contents of
`index.html`'s `<body>` and import your component:

```html
<body>
  <main>
    <h1>My first Gyral app</h1>
    <my-counter></my-counter>
  </main>
  <script type="module" src="/src/counter.ts"></script>
</body>
```

Run `npm run dev` and open the address it prints. The counter is a standard custom element with
its own Shadow DOM, so it works in any page and alongside any framework.

When the page loads an entry module instead (the `basic` template's `src/main.ts`), that module
must import every component module, for its side effect. Each new component in its own file
gets a line here, such as the stepper below:

```ts
// src/main.ts
import './counter.js';
import './stepper.js';
```

A module that nothing imports never runs, so its tag is never defined: `<my-stepper>` stays an
empty unknown element. In development, Gyral warns in the console (G0014) when a tag on the page
is still undefined 3 seconds after it loaded; production builds stay silent. A component that renders another
component in its view imports that module too.

## Read input

Intents get more than the event. Here's a step size the user can type. `on('input', parser)`
gives the parser the number input's `valueAsNumber` (`undefined` while the field is empty or
invalid), and the parser checks it before it reaches the model:

```ts
// src/stepper.ts
import { define, html, on } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly count: number;
  readonly step: number;
}

export type Msg =
  { readonly _tag: 'Increment' } | { readonly _tag: 'StepChanged'; readonly step: number };

export const Stepper = define<State, Msg>()('my-stepper', {
  init: () => ({ count: 0, step: 1 }),
  intent: {
    Increment: () => ({ _tag: 'Increment' }),
    // Not a whole number: ignore the keystroke, keep the last good step.
    StepChanged: on('input', ({ valueAsNumber: step }) =>
      step !== undefined && Number.isInteger(step) ? { _tag: 'StepChanged', step } : undefined,
    ),
  },
  update: {
    Increment: (s) => ({ ...s, count: s.count + s.step }),
    StepChanged: (s, m) => ({ ...s, step: m.step }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <label for="step">Step</label>
    <input id="step" type="number" value=${s.step} data-intent=${i.StepChanged} />
    <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Increment}>Add ${s.step}</button>
    <output aria-live="polite">${s.count}</output>
  `,
});
```

The model only ever sees a whole number. Parsing happens once, at the boundary, which is where
Gyral wants it.

## Test it

`update` is a plain function, so you can test behaviour without a browser. `@gyral/testing`
gives you `step` (one message) and `run` (a sequence):

```sh
npm install -D @gyral/testing vitest
```

```ts
// src/counter.test.ts
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { run, step } from '@gyral/testing';
import { Counter } from './counter.js';

it('counts', () => {
  expect(step(Counter.spec, { count: 1 }, { _tag: 'Increment' }).state).toEqual({ count: 2 });

  const { state } = run(Counter.spec, [
    { _tag: 'Increment' },
    { _tag: 'Increment' },
    { _tag: 'Decrement' },
  ]);
  expect(state.count).toBe(1);
});
```

`Counter.spec` is the object you passed to `define()`. Tests that need the real element (clicks,
focus, rendering) run in a browser with [Vitest browser mode](https://vitest.dev/guide/browser/)
and `await settled()` before they look at the DOM; `@gyral/testing` also has helpers for server
rendering, hydration and virtual time. See [Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/).

  [signup form with validation](https://gyral.dev/docs/recipes/#a-signup-form-with-native-validation), each a
  complete component with tests that needs nothing beyond a `basic` app.
- Learn the three parts in depth: [Intent](https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/), [Model and update](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/)
  and [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/).
- Browse the [examples](https://gyral.dev/examples/): forms, HTTP, routing, shared state and server rendering.
- See a whole application in [gyral-shop](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral-shop).
- Before you ship, read [Deploying](https://gyral.dev/docs/deploying/) and the
  [known issues](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#known-issues).
- Working with a coding agent? Connect it to Gyral's MCP server and skill:
  [Use Gyral with coding agents](https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/).
- Upgrading an existing app? [Versioning and stability](https://gyral.dev/docs/versioning/) explains how to move
  to 0.3.8 safely.

# Recipes

> Complete components to copy, with their tests. A todo list with filters, a signup form with native validation, and fixes for common bugs.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/recipes/

Each recipe is a whole component in one file, with its tests. They need only `@gyral/core`,
plus `@gyral/testing` and Vitest for the tests, so they work in a new `basic` app from
[create-gyral](https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/#create-a-project). Every recipe compiles against Gyral
0.3.8, and the site tests each one in a browser when it builds.

## A todo list with filters

Add todos, tick them off, delete them, and show all, active or done ones:

```ts
// src/todo-app.ts
import { define, each, focus, html, intentsOf, type TemplateResult } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Todo {
  readonly id: number;
  readonly text: string;
  readonly done: boolean;
}

export type Filter = 'all' | 'active' | 'done';

export interface State {
  readonly todos: readonly Todo[];
  readonly nextId: number;
  readonly draft: string;
  readonly filter: Filter;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Typed'; readonly text: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Add'; readonly text: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Toggle'; readonly id: number }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Delete'; readonly id: number }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Show'; readonly filter: Filter };

const FILTERS: readonly Filter[] = ['all', 'active', 'done'];
const LABELS: Readonly<Record<Filter, string>> = { all: 'All', active: 'Active', done: 'Done' };

const isFilter = (value: string | undefined): value is Filter => FILTERS.some((f) => f === value);

/** A row's id from its control's `value`, or `undefined` for anything else. */
const idOf = (value: string | undefined): number | undefined =>
  value !== undefined && /^\d+$/.test(value) ? Number(value) : undefined;

/** The todos a filter shows. State keeps the whole list; the view shows this. */
export const visible = (todos: readonly Todo[], filter: Filter): readonly Todo[] =>
  filter === 'all' ? todos : todos.filter((t) => t.done === (filter === 'done'));

// The intent names as a module constant, so rows can use them and stay pure.
const i = intentsOf<typeof TodoApp>();

// A row reads only its todo and module constants. Its controls carry the id, never a position.
const Row = (todo: Todo): TemplateResult =>
  html`<li>
    <label>
      <input type="checkbox" value=${todo.id} ?checked=${todo.done} data-intent=${i.Toggle} />
      ${todo.text}
    </label>
    <button
      type="button"
      value=${todo.id}
      aria-label=${`Delete ${todo.text}`}
      data-intent=${i.Delete}
    >
      Delete
    </button>
  </li>`;

export const TodoApp = define<State, Msg>()('my-todo-app', {
  init: () => ({ todos: [], nextId: 1, draft: '', filter: 'all' }),
  intent: {
    Typed: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Typed', text: value ?? '' }),
    Add: ({ formData }) => {
      const text = formData?.get('text');
      return typeof text === 'string' && text.trim() !== ''
        ? { _tag: 'Add', text: text.trim() }
        : undefined;
    },
    Toggle: ({ value }) => {
      const id = idOf(value);
      return id === undefined ? undefined : { _tag: 'Toggle', id };
    },
    Delete: ({ value }) => {
      const id = idOf(value);
      return id === undefined ? undefined : { _tag: 'Delete', id };
    },
    Show: ({ value }) => (isFilter(value) ? { _tag: 'Show', filter: value } : undefined),
  },
  update: {
    Typed: (s, m) => ({ ...s, draft: m.text }),
    // Clearing `draft` empties the input; focus goes back to it for the next todo.
    Add: (s, m) => [
      {
        ...s,
        todos: [...s.todos, { id: s.nextId, text: m.text, done: false }],
        nextId: s.nextId + 1,
        draft: '',
      },
      [focus('#new-todo')],
    ],
    Toggle: (s, m) => ({
      ...s,
      todos: s.todos.map((t) => (t.id === m.id ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)),
    }),
    // The deleted row had focus: give it to the input, not to the page body.
    Delete: (s, m) => [{ ...s, todos: s.todos.filter((t) => t.id !== m.id) }, [focus('#new-todo')]],
    Show: (s, m) => ({ ...s, filter: m.filter }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => {
    const shown = visible(s.todos, s.filter);
    const left = s.todos.filter((t) => !t.done).length;
    return html`
      <form data-intent=${i.Add}>
        <label for="new-todo">New todo</label>
        <input
          id="new-todo"
          name="text"
          autocomplete="off"
          value=${s.draft}
          data-intent=${i.Typed}
        />
        <button>Add</button>
      </form>
      <div role="group" aria-label="Show">
        ${FILTERS.map(
          (f) =>
            html`<button
              type="button"
              value=${f}
              aria-pressed=${s.filter === f}
              data-intent=${i.Show}
            >
              ${LABELS[f]}
            </button>`,
        )}
      </div>
      <ul aria-label="Todos">
        ${each(shown, (t) => t.id, Row)}
      </ul>
      <p>${shown.length === 0 ? 'Nothing to show.' : ''}</p>
      <p><output aria-live="polite">${left} left</output></p>
    `;
  },
});
```

How it works:

- **State keeps the whole list. The view filters it.** `visible(todos, filter)` is a plain
  function that the view and the tests call. The filter is state; the filtered list isn't, so
  the two can't get out of step.
- **Controls carry the id**: `value=${todo.id}`, and the parser reads `value`. A message says
  which todo, never which row. See
  [the wrong item changes](#toggling-an-item-in-a-filtered-list-changes-the-wrong-item).
- **Rows are keyed by id**: `each(shown, (t) => t.id, Row)`. A todo keeps its element when the
  filter changes or another row goes away.
- **Rows are pure.** `Row` reads only its todo and module constants, such as
  `i = intentsOf<typeof TodoApp>()`. Its return type is written out, so `Row` and `TodoApp`
  don't infer each other's types. The view uses its own `i`.
- **The input is form state.** `value=${s.draft}` follows `Typed`, and `Add` sets `draft` back
  to `''`, which empties the input. Without `draft` in state, the text would stay after Add.
- **Focus is a command.** `Add` and `Delete` return `focus('#new-todo')`, so focus never falls
  to the page body when its row is deleted.
- The filter buttons use `.map`: three buttons that never move don't need `each`.

Test the model without a browser. `run` folds messages from `init` (or from `state`), and
`parse` runs one parser without a DOM:

```ts
// src/todo-app.test.ts
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { focusTargetsIn, parse, run, step } from '@gyral/testing';
import { TodoApp, visible } from './todo-app.js';

const added = run(TodoApp.spec, [
  { _tag: 'Add', text: 'Write docs' },
  { _tag: 'Add', text: 'Ship it' },
  { _tag: 'Add', text: 'Celebrate' },
]).state;

it('adds todos with their own ids and clears the input', () => {
  expect(added.todos.map((t) => [t.id, t.text])).toEqual([
    [1, 'Write docs'],
    [2, 'Ship it'],
    [3, 'Celebrate'],
  ]);
  expect(added.draft).toBe('');
  const { commands } = step(TodoApp.spec, added, { _tag: 'Add', text: 'More' });
  expect(focusTargetsIn(commands)).toEqual([{ selector: '#new-todo' }]);
});

it('toggles and deletes by id, whatever the filter shows', () => {
  const { state } = run(
    TodoApp.spec,
    [
      { _tag: 'Toggle', id: 1 },
      { _tag: 'Show', filter: 'active' },
      // "Celebrate" is the second row on screen now, but the message names it by id.
      { _tag: 'Toggle', id: 3 },
      { _tag: 'Delete', id: 2 },
    ],
    { state: added },
  );
  expect(state.todos).toEqual([
    { id: 1, text: 'Write docs', done: true },
    { id: 3, text: 'Celebrate', done: true },
  ]);
  expect(visible(state.todos, 'active')).toEqual([]);
  expect(visible(state.todos, 'done').map((t) => t.id)).toEqual([1, 3]);
});

it('reads ids and filters from the markup, and ignores anything else', () => {
  expect(parse(TodoApp, 'Toggle', { value: '3' })).toEqual({ _tag: 'Toggle', id: 3 });
  expect(parse(TodoApp, 'Toggle', { value: 'three' })).toBeUndefined();
  expect(parse(TodoApp, 'Show', { value: 'done' })).toEqual({ _tag: 'Show', filter: 'done' });
  expect(parse(TodoApp, 'Show', { value: 'archived' })).toBeUndefined();
});
```

## A signup form with native validation

No extra packages. The browser's constraint checks find what is wrong, and your own messages
say it. The [Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/#complete-example-a-validated-form) page starts with this same
component and explains each part; here it comes with its tests:

```ts
// src/account-form.ts
import { define, focus, html } from '@gyral/core';

/** The fields, in the order they appear: the first one with an error gets focus. */
export const FIELDS = ['name', 'email', 'password', 'consent'] as const;
export type Field = (typeof FIELDS)[number];

/** One message per field; `''` means no error. */
export type Errors = Readonly<Record<Field, string>>;

export const NO_ERRORS: Errors = { name: '', email: '', password: '', consent: '' };

export interface State {
  readonly errors: Errors;
  /** What the live region announces after a rejected submit; `''` otherwise. */
  readonly summary: string;
  /** The clean values after a successful signup. */
  readonly account: { readonly name: string; readonly email: string } | undefined;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Rejected'; readonly errors: Errors }
  | { readonly _tag: 'SignedUp'; readonly name: string; readonly email: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Checked'; readonly field: Field; readonly error: string };

const isField = (name: string): name is Field => FIELDS.some((f) => f === name);

/**
 * Your message for a field's first problem, from the browser's own checks (`validity`), or
 * `''` when the field is fine. The constraints in the markup (`required`, `type="email"`,
 * `minlength`) still decide what is wrong; `novalidate` only stops the browser from
 * blocking the submit and showing its own bubble.
 */
export function problemWith(input: HTMLInputElement): string {
  const { validity } = input;
  // A checkbox is missing when unchecked. `required` accepts "   ", so blank text is missing too.
  const missing =
    input.type === 'checkbox' ? !input.checked : validity.valueMissing || input.value.trim() === '';
  switch (input.name) {
    case 'name':
      return missing ? 'Enter your name.' : '';
    case 'email':
      if (missing) return 'Enter your email address.';
      return validity.typeMismatch ? 'Enter an email address like ada@example.com.' : '';
    case 'password':
      if (missing) return 'Enter a password.';
      // `tooShort` is set only for typed values; the length check also covers a pre-filled one.
      return validity.tooShort || input.value.length < input.minLength
        ? 'Use at least 8 characters.'
        : '';
    case 'consent':
      return missing ? 'Accept the privacy policy to continue.' : '';
    default:
      return '';
  }
}

/** What the status region announces after a successful signup. */
const welcome = (account: State['account']): string =>
  account === undefined ? '' : `Welcome, ${account.name}! We’ll write to ${account.email}.`;

/** Reads a submitted form: every field's error, or the clean values. */
function submission(form: Element, data: FormData | undefined): Msg | undefined {
  if (!(form instanceof HTMLFormElement) || data === undefined) return undefined;
  const errors: Record<Field, string> = { ...NO_ERRORS };
  for (const field of FIELDS) {
    const input = form.elements.namedItem(field);
    if (input instanceof HTMLInputElement) errors[field] = problemWith(input);
  }
  if (FIELDS.some((f) => errors[f] !== '')) return { _tag: 'Rejected', errors };
  const text = (field: Field): string => {
    const value = data.get(field);
    return typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : '';
  };
  // The password stays in the form data: never keep it in state.
  return { _tag: 'SignedUp', name: text('name'), email: text('email') };
}

export const AccountForm = define<State, Msg>()('my-account-form', {
  init: () => ({ errors: NO_ERRORS, summary: '', account: undefined }),
  intent: {
    // Not a message tag, so it may return either message.
    Submit: ({ target, formData }) => submission(target, formData),
    // Text fields send it on `input`, the checkbox on `change`.
    Checked: ({ target }) =>
      target instanceof HTMLInputElement && isField(target.name)
        ? { _tag: 'Checked', field: target.name, error: problemWith(target) }
        : undefined,
  },
  update: {
    // Show every error at once, announce how many, and focus the first field that has one.
    Rejected: (s, m) => {
      const count = FIELDS.filter((f) => m.errors[f] !== '').length;
      const first = FIELDS.find((f) => m.errors[f] !== '');
      const summary = `Fix ${String(count)} ${count === 1 ? 'field' : 'fields'} to continue.`;
      const focusFirst = first === undefined ? [] : [focus(`#${first}`)];
      return [{ ...s, errors: m.errors, summary }, focusFirst];
    },
    // In an app, this also returns the command that posts the form.
    SignedUp: (_s, m) => ({
      errors: NO_ERRORS,
      summary: '',
      account: { name: m.name, email: m.email },
    }),
    // While the user types, only a field that already shows an error is checked again,
    // so a message changes or disappears as soon as the value is fixed.
    Checked: (s, m) =>
      s.errors[m.field] === '' ? s : { ...s, errors: { ...s.errors, [m.field]: m.error } },
  },
  // No `value` bindings: what the user typed stays in the fields after a rejected submit.
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <form novalidate data-intent=${i.Submit}>
      <p role="alert">${s.summary}</p>

      <label for="name">Name</label>
      <input
        id="name"
        name="name"
        autocomplete="name"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.name !== ''}
        aria-describedby="name-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="name-error">${s.errors.name}</p>

      <label for="email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        autocomplete="email"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.email !== ''}
        aria-describedby="email-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="email-error">${s.errors.email}</p>

      <label for="password">Password</label>
      <input
        id="password"
        name="password"
        type="password"
        autocomplete="new-password"
        required
        minlength="8"
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.password !== ''}
        aria-describedby="password-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="password-error">${s.errors.password}</p>

      <input
        id="consent"
        name="consent"
        type="checkbox"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.consent !== ''}
        aria-describedby="consent-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <label for="consent">I accept the privacy policy</label>
      <p id="consent-error">${s.errors.consent}</p>

      <button>Create account</button>
    </form>
    <p role="status">${welcome(s.account)}</p>
  `,
});
```

How it works:

- **`novalidate` on the form, constraints on the fields.** `required`, `type="email"` and
  `minlength` still set each field's `validity`. `novalidate` stops the browser from blocking
  the submit. Without it, a failing constraint shows the browser's bubble and no `submit` event
  fires, so your messages never appear.
- **The submit parser reads `validity`.** `problemWith(input)` turns `valueMissing`,
  `typeMismatch`, `tooShort` and an unchecked checkbox into your words. `Submit` checks every
  field and returns `Rejected` with all the errors, or `SignedUp` with clean values. Reading the
  form is input parsing, the intent layer's job; reducers see only the result.
- **Check what the browser doesn't.** `required` accepts a name made of spaces, so the parser
  trims first. `tooShort` is set only after the user types, not for a value set by script or
  rendered by a server, so the parser checks the length too.
- **Errors are state**: one string per field, `''` for none. The view writes `aria-invalid` and
  the message, and `aria-describedby` links the message to its field.
- **Focus goes to the first invalid field**, through a `focus()` command from `Rejected`,
  and the `role="alert"` paragraph announces how many fields to fix.
- **An error clears as soon as the field is fixed.** Each field sends `Checked` on input (the
  checkbox on change). The reducer updates only a field that already shows an error, so nothing
  turns red while someone is still typing.
- **Enter submits.** The form has a submit button, so Enter in any field submits it, like a
  click.
- **No password in state.** `SignedUp` carries the name and the email. To send the form to a
  server, keep the raw `FormData` in the message and post it with a command, as in
  [Submitting to the server](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/#submitting-to-the-server).

The reducers are tested without a browser:

```ts
// src/account-form.test.ts
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { focusTargetsIn, run, step } from '@gyral/testing';
import { AccountForm, NO_ERRORS } from './account-form.js';

const rejected = {
  name: '',
  email: 'Enter an email address like ada@example.com.',
  password: 'Use at least 8 characters.',
  consent: '',
};

it('shows every error, announces how many and focuses the first invalid field', () => {
  const { state, commands } = step(
    AccountForm.spec,
    { errors: NO_ERRORS, summary: '', account: undefined },
    { _tag: 'Rejected', errors: rejected },
  );
  expect(state.errors).toEqual(rejected);
  expect(state.summary).toBe('Fix 2 fields to continue.');
  expect(focusTargetsIn(commands)).toEqual([{ selector: '#email' }]);
});

it('clears an error as soon as the field is fixed, and leaves untouched fields alone', () => {
  const { state } = run(AccountForm.spec, [
    { _tag: 'Rejected', errors: rejected },
    { _tag: 'Checked', field: 'email', error: '' },
    { _tag: 'Checked', field: 'name', error: 'Enter your name.' },
  ]);
  expect(state.errors).toEqual({ ...rejected, email: '' });
});

it('welcomes the new user and forgets old errors', () => {
  const { state } = run(AccountForm.spec, [
    { _tag: 'Rejected', errors: rejected },
    { _tag: 'SignedUp', name: 'Ada', email: 'ada@example.com' },
  ]);
  expect(state).toEqual({
    errors: NO_ERRORS,
    summary: '',
    account: { name: 'Ada', email: 'ada@example.com' },
  });
});
```

The submit parser reads the form's fields, so test it in a browser too. In a `basic` app,
`npm test` runs both files in Chromium. `mount()` sets values with script, which is why the
parser's own length check matters:

```ts
// src/account-form.browser.test.ts
import { expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { mount } from '@gyral/testing';
import { AccountForm } from './account-form.js';

it('reads the browser’s checks on submit and focuses the first invalid field', async () => {
  const form = await mount(AccountForm);
  await form.type('#email', 'ada');
  await form.type('#password', 'short');
  await form.click('button');

  expect(form.$('[role="alert"]')?.textContent).toBe('Fix 4 fields to continue.');
  expect(form.$('#name-error')?.textContent).toBe('Enter your name.');
  expect(form.$('#email-error')?.textContent).toBe('Enter an email address like ada@example.com.');
  expect(form.$('#password-error')?.textContent).toBe('Use at least 8 characters.');
  expect(form.$('#consent-error')?.textContent).toBe('Accept the privacy policy to continue.');
  expect(form.el.shadowRoot?.activeElement?.id).toBe('name');

  await form.type('#name', '  Ada  ');
  expect(form.$('#name-error')?.textContent).toBe('');
  await form.type('#email', 'ada@example.com');
  await form.type('#password', 'correct horse');
  await form.click('#consent');
  expect(form.$('#consent-error')?.textContent).toBe('');
  await form.click('button');
  expect(form.$('[role="status"]')?.textContent).toBe(
    'Welcome, Ada! We’ll write to ada@example.com.',
  );
  form.dispose();
});
```

To validate on the server with the same rules, use one schema for both sides:
[Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/#one-schema-for-both-sides).

## Troubleshooting

### Toggling an item in a filtered list changes the wrong item

**What you see.** With a filter on, ticking a row ticks a different item, often one that isn't
shown.

**Why.** The control carries the row's position, and the reducer uses it as an index into the
whole list:

```ts
// Wrong: in the view, `n` is the row's place in the filtered list…
${visible(s.todos, s.filter).map(
  (t, n) => html`<input type="checkbox" value=${n} data-intent=${i.Toggle} />`,
)}

// …and the reducer reads it as a place in the whole list.
Toggle: (s, m) => ({
  ...s,
  todos: s.todos.map((t, n) => (n === m.index ? { ...t, done: !t.done } : t)),
}),
```

With "Active" showing, the second row on screen may be the fourth todo, so the reducer changes
`s.todos[1]` instead. A sort or a search breaks it the same way.

**Fix.** Carry the id, and find the item by id:

- Put `value=${todo.id}` on the control, and parse `value` as an id.
- Match by id in the reducer: `t.id === m.id`.
- Key the list by id: `each(shown, (t) => t.id, Row)`.

A key alone doesn't fix it. The key keeps each element with its item; the message still has to
say which item. The [todo list](#a-todo-list-with-filters) recipe does all three.

### Custom error messages never show

**What you see.** Submitting an empty form shows the browser's bubble ("Please fill out this
field"), and your parser never runs.

**Why.** Without `novalidate`, the browser checks `required`, `type="email"`, `minlength` and
`pattern` before it fires `submit`. When one fails, there is no `submit` event, so there is no
intent.

**Fix.** Add `novalidate` to the `<form>` and keep the constraints on the fields. Read each
field's `validity` in the submit parser, as the
[signup form](#a-signup-form-with-native-validation) does.

---

# Use Gyral with coding agents

> Connect Claude Code, VS Code or any MCP client to the Gyral MCP server, hosted or local, install the agent skill, and give agents llms-small.txt.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/

A coding agent writes better Gyral code when it can look things up instead of guessing. Gyral
gives agents four things, and they work together:

- **The MCP server**, `@gyral/mcp`: searches these docs, returns exact API signatures and
  working examples, scaffolds components, and typechecks code against your project. It runs
  locally or at `https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp`.
- **The agent skill**: the rules and the API in a form agents load on demand.
- **[llms-small.txt](https://gyral.dev/llms-small.txt)**: the rules, one complete component and tested recipes
  in one small file.
- **An `AGENTS.md`** in every app `create-gyral` makes.

## The hosted MCP server

`https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp` is a public MCP server over Streamable HTTP. It needs no token and
no install, and it only reads: it answers from Gyral's docs, API and examples.

In Claude Code:

```sh
claude mcp add --transport http gyral https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp
```

In VS Code, add it to `.vscode/mcp.json`:

```json
{ "servers": { "gyral": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp" } } }
```

Any other client that speaks Streamable HTTP: add a server with the URL
`https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp` and no authentication.

The hosted server has every tool except `check_snippet`, which needs your project's
TypeScript and packages. It can run an older `@gyral/mcp` than the latest release; its
`initialize` response and `https://mcp.gyral.dev/healthz` report the version it serves. This
page describes the tools as `@gyral/mcp` 0.3.8 provides them.

## The local MCP server

Run the server on your machine when the agent writes code. It adds `check_snippet`, which
typechecks against the TypeScript and `@gyral/*` versions installed in your project
(TypeScript 5 or 6; TypeScript 7 has no compiler API, so there it asks you to run your own
typecheck), and
`scaffold_component` reads your `package.json`. Start it from the project directory:

```sh
claude mcp add gyral -- npx -y @gyral/mcp
```

That's Claude Code. Other clients:

- **Codex**: `codex mcp add gyral -- npx -y @gyral/mcp`
- **Cursor**, in `.cursor/mcp.json`:

  ```json
  { "mcpServers": { "gyral": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@gyral/mcp"] } } }
  ```

- **VS Code**, in `.vscode/mcp.json`:

  ```json
  { "servers": { "gyral": { "type": "stdio", "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@gyral/mcp"] } } }
  ```

- **Any other client**: run `npx -y @gyral/mcp` as a stdio server.

npx fetches the latest `@gyral/mcp` release unless your project has another version installed.

The local server answers from the docs bundled with its own version, so it works offline and
matches the Gyral you install. Set `GYRAL_DOCS_URL=https://gyral.dev/llms-full.txt` to load
the latest docs at startup instead; it falls back to the bundled copy after 3 seconds.
`GYRAL_PROJECT_DIR` points `check_snippet` at another directory than the working one.

## The tools

| Tool                 | What it returns                                                                                                            |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `start_here`         | The mental model, the rules, the workflow, and which example or guide covers which task                                    |
| `search_docs`        | Ranked doc sections for a query: title, URL and snippet                                                                    |
| `get_doc`            | One docs page, or one section with `#anchor`, such as `forms#the-server-half`                                              |
| `get_api`            | The declaration, doc comment and import line of an export, with usage code and the next call; on a miss, the nearest names |
| `list_examples`      | Every example and what it shows                                                                                            |
| `get_example`        | One example's component source                                                                                             |
| `scaffold_component` | Starting code: `basic`, `form`, `form-native` or `ssr-page`, importing only what you have                                  |
| `check_snippet`      | Type errors for a module against your project, with a suggested fix for each (local only)                                  |

The workflow the server teaches, first in its instructions and in every tool description: call
`start_here` once, start from `get_example` or `scaffold_component`, write the module right
away, then run `check_snippet` and apply its suggested fixes until it passes. Use `get_api` only
for a name you already saw in an example or an error, not to read the API type by type.

`get_api` steers back to that loop. On a function with a matching example, such as
`define`, `each`, `fieldErrors` or `every`, it adds a short usage module and the call that gives
working code for the task, such as `scaffold_component({ tag: "signup-form", kind: "form-native" })`.
On a type, it adds a note that TypeScript infers it and that the real type errors come from
`check_snippet` (on the local server) or your typecheck. `get_api("*")` groups the functions by task, with the example or scaffold to start from,
and collapses the types into one line. The local stdio server also counts reads (every docs, API and example lookup) since the
agent last called `scaffold_component` or `check_snippet`: from the third `get_example`, the
fourth `get_api` or the eighth read of any kind, its answers end with a nudge that names the
examples read and suggests adapting the closest one, then `check_snippet`. The HTTP server, hosted or your own, keeps no
state between requests, so it never nudges.

`scaffold_component` imports only packages your project has installed, and
writes a model test only when `@gyral/testing` and `vitest` are there. `form-native` needs no
dependencies: it turns the browser's own constraint checks into your messages. `check_snippet`
also flags Gyral mistakes TypeScript can't see, such as a one-call `define` or side effects in
`update`.

The server also offers the resources `gyral://llms.txt`, `gyral://skill` and
`gyral://skill/references/{name}`, and a `build-gyral-component` prompt.

### Host your own

`gyral-mcp http` runs the server behind the hosted one: read-only, anonymous Streamable HTTP
at `/mcp`, without `check_snippet`. It listens on `127.0.0.1:3000` by default, and needs
`GYRAL_MCP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` set to the origin it's served from:

```sh
GYRAL_MCP_PUBLIC_ORIGIN=http://127.0.0.1:3000 npx -y @gyral/mcp http
```

It is configured by environment variables only; `gyral-mcp http --help` lists them. Put it
behind TLS, and pin the package version you deploy. The
[package README](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/v0.3.8/packages/mcp/README.md#public-hosting)
has the details.

## The agent skill

The skill teaches an agent the rules and the API, with a reference per topic that it loads
when the task needs it. Every code block in it typechecks against the packages.
`SKILL.md` opens with where to start from working code (the recipes, llms-small.txt and the MCP
loop) and the rule that the entry must import every component module, and its forms reference
starts with native validation, as the [Forms guide](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/) does.

In Claude Code, add Gyral's repository as a plugin marketplace and install the plugin:

```text
/plugin marketplace add gyraljs/gyral
/plugin install gyral@gyral
```

From a shell: `claude plugin marketplace add gyraljs/gyral && claude plugin install gyral@gyral`.

To keep the skill in the project itself, for every agent that works on it, let `@gyral/mcp`
write it. Run it from the app's directory, with the version of `@gyral/core` the app has
installed:

```sh
npx @gyral/mcp@0.3.8 skill           # write the skill into the project
npx @gyral/mcp@0.3.8 skill --check   # in CI: fail when a copy differs
```

`skill` writes `SKILL.md` and its references to `.claude/skills/gyral`, and to
`.agents/skills/gyral` when that folder exists (`--dir <folder>` names others), and removes files
the skill no longer has. The version must match the installed `@gyral/core`, because each
release's skill describes that release; it says which command to run when it doesn't. With
`--check` it writes nothing and exits 1 when a copy differs, so a CI job catches a skill left
behind by an upgrade.

Other agents: copy
[`skills/gyral/`](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/tree/v0.3.8/skills/gyral) into the agent's
skills or rules folder, or point it at `SKILL.md`.

## Docs for agents

- **[llms-small.txt](https://gyral.dev/llms-small.txt)**: read first. The mental model, MUST and DO NOT rules, a
  complete component with tests, the recipes, and where each export comes from, in under
  40 KB. Every code block in it compiles against the released packages.
- **[llms.txt](https://gyral.dev/llms.txt)**: the index of every page, each with a line on when to read it.
- **[llms-full.txt](https://gyral.dev/llms-full.txt)**: all the docs, the API reference and the examples in one
  file.
- Every docs page has a Markdown copy: add `index.md` to its URL, as in
  `/docs/testing/index.md`.

## New apps

`npm create gyral@latest` writes an `AGENTS.md` into every project, and a `CLAUDE.md` that
imports it, so an agent that opens the project learns the rules and the commands before it
writes anything. See [Getting started](https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/#create-a-project).

---

# Components

> How define() turns a spec into a custom element, and how components pass data to each other with props and outputs.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/components/

A Gyral component is a standard custom element. You don't write a class: you describe the
component as data, and `define()` builds the element, a plain `HTMLElement` subclass. This page covers the parts of that
description, then how components talk to each other: **props down, outputs up**.

## Anatomy of define()

```ts
// src/greeter.ts
import { define, html } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly name: string;
}

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'NameChanged'; readonly name: string };

export const Greeter = define<State, Msg>()('my-greeter', {
  init: () => ({ name: '' }),
  intent: {
    NameChanged: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'NameChanged', name: value ?? '' }),
  },
  update: {
    NameChanged: (s, m) => ({ ...s, name: m.name.trim() }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <label for="name">Your name</label>
    <input id="name" autocomplete="given-name" data-intent=${i.NameChanged} />
    <p>${s.name === '' ? 'Hello!' : `Hello, ${s.name}!`}</p>
  `,
});
```

`define<State, Msg>()(tag, spec)` registers `<my-greeter>` and returns its class. It is two
calls: the first takes the types you write (state, messages, props, outputs), the second the
tag and spec, so TypeScript can still infer the intent names from the spec's `intent` keys. A
component needs `init` and `view`; `intent` and `update` come with messages, and the rest is
optional:

| Part            | What it is                                                                                                     | Guide                                                                                                 |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `init`          | The starting state, computed from props. May also start one-shot commands.                                     | [Model and update](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/)                                                                     |
| `subscriptions` | The long-running commands that should be running for this state and props (clocks, feeds, watches).            | [Subscriptions](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/#subscriptions)                                                          |
| `intent`        | Parsers that turn platform events into messages. Their keys are the component's intent names.                  | [Intent](https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/)                                                                               |
| `update`        | One pure reducer per message tag: state in, next state (and commands) out.                                     | [Model and update](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/)                                                                     |
| `view`          | A pure function from state to an `html` template that _names_ intents.                                         | [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/)                                                                                 |
| `props`         | Inputs from the parent or from attributes, declared with `prop.*` builders.                                    | [below](#props)                                                                                       |
| `styles`        | Shadow-root CSS: `css` values or strings.                                                                      | [Styling](https://gyral.dev/docs/styling/)                                                                             |
| `stores`        | Shared state the component reads.                                                                              | [Shared state](https://gyral.dev/docs/stores/)                                                                         |
| `shadow`        | `false` renders into light DOM; `{ delegatesFocus: true }` passes focus to the first focusable element inside. | [Styling](https://gyral.dev/docs/styling/#light-dom-components), [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#focusing-into-a-child-component) |
| `hydrate`       | When a server-rendered instance hydrates: `load`, `idle`, `visible`, `interaction`.                            | [Server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/)                                                           |

A few more optional fields cover rarer needs: `error` (a fallback view, see
[Error handling](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/)), `states`
(custom states for CSS, see [Styling](https://gyral.dev/docs/styling/#custom-states)), `viewTransition` (render a
change inside a View Transition, see [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#view-transitions)), `renderOnFrame`
(message tags from bursty sources, such as a socket feed or a sensor, that render once per
animation frame), and `formAssociated` (a component that takes part in a native form, see
[Custom form controls](https://gyral.dev/docs/form-associated/)).

The type parameters are the contract. `State` is a plain data record (JSON, when the component
is [server-rendered](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/#loading-components-in-the-browser)), `Msg` a union of tagged objects, and TypeScript checks that `update` has a reducer for every tag and that the view
only names intents that exist.

`define()` registers the tag when its module runs, so the page's entry module (or a module it
imports) must import every component module: `import './greeter.js';` in `src/main.ts`. A
component module that nothing imports never runs, and its tag stays an empty unknown element;
development builds warn (G0014) when a tag is still undefined 3 seconds after the page loaded. A parent that renders a child imports it too, as `Total` imports `Stepper`
[below](#child-components-and-outputs).

`define()` returns the element class. Its `spec` property is the object you passed in, which is
how [tests](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/) run `update` without a DOM. Export it as
`export const Greeter = define…`, and `gyral()`, Gyral's Vite plugins, writes `HTMLElementTagNameMap` entries for
every such component into `.gyral/elements.d.ts` (list that file in your tsconfig's `include`),
so `document.querySelector('my-greeter')` is typed with no declaration of your own. It reads
calls in code, not in comments or strings. For `tsc` outside Vite, the
`gyral-types` command writes the same file.

## Props

Props are the component's inputs. Declare each one with a `prop` builder. A builder says how
an attribute's string becomes a value, and a prop whose type can't be `undefined` must say how a
value is guaranteed: `required` or `default`.

```ts
// src/badge.ts
import { define, html, prop, type Stateless } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Props {
  readonly label: string;
  readonly count: number;
  readonly note: string | undefined;
}

export const Badge = define<Stateless, never, Props>()('my-badge', {
  props: {
    label: prop.string({ required: true }),
    count: prop.number({ default: 0 }),
    note: prop.string(),
  },
  intent: {},
  update: {},
  view: (_s, _i, { props }) => html`
    <span>${props.label}: <data value=${props.count}>${props.count}</data></span>
    ${props.note === undefined ? '' : html`<small>${props.note}</small>`}
  `,
});
```

- **Read props as context.** Every reducer and the view get `{ props }` as their last argument.
  Don't copy props into state just to read them.
- **`required: true`** is a promise from the parent. A missing value logs one warning per
  instance at first render.
- **`default`** is used whenever the element's own value is missing.
- A component with no state of its own uses `Stateless` and can leave out `init`.
- Don't name a prop after a built-in element property such as `hidden`, `title` or `id`. It is
  an error in development, because the prop would replace the platform's behaviour.

### Builders and attributes

| Builder                     | The attribute is parsed with           | Attribute name         |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------- | ---------------------- |
| `prop.string(opts?)`        | nothing: the string as is              | kebab-case of the prop |
| `prop.number(opts?)`        | `Number(v)`; empty or `NaN` is invalid | kebab-case             |
| `prop.boolean(opts?)`       | present is `true`, absent is `false`   | kebab-case             |
| `prop.json(schema, opts?)`  | `JSON.parse`, then the schema          | kebab-case             |
| `prop.value(schema, opts?)` | no attribute: set it as a property     | none                   |

A prop named `maxValue` reads the attribute `max-value`; pass `attribute: 'name'` to choose
another, or `attribute: false` for a property only. The options are `required`, `default`,
`attribute` and `schema`, and `equals` for `prop.json` and `prop.value`
([below](#when-a-prop-counts-as-changed)). Templates write that attribute name: HTML lowercases
attribute names, so `maxValue=${n}` on a custom element would set `maxvalue`, which no prop
reads, and the build and ESLint report it. Write `max-value=${n}`, or set the property with
`.maxValue=${n}`. Development also warns ([G0024](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0024)) when a page's HTML or a
host framework writes the lowercased name.

A prop can't take the name of a member every element already has: a built-in property such as
`hidden` or `title`, which would change what the platform does, or one of Gyral's, `state`,
`send`, `drivers`, `stores` and `initialMessages`, which would hide the component's model.
TypeScript rejects the name and development throws ([G0023](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0023)). Rename the
property, and keep the attribute if pages use it: `badge: prop.string({ attribute: 'state' })`.

The schemas are [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev), so any library that implements it
works: valibot, zod, ArkType. `string`, `number` and `boolean` carry tiny built-in schemas, so
simple props need no library; pass `schema` to narrow one, such as
`prop.string({ schema: v.picklist(['asc', 'desc']), default: 'asc' })`.

Attributes are strings from outside your code, so they are **always validated**. An invalid
value is logged with the tag, the prop and the schema's issues, then treated as missing, so its
`default` applies. Property sets come from typed code and are validated in development only.
Props never write attributes back; state that CSS needs goes through
[custom states](https://gyral.dev/docs/styling/#custom-states).

### Objects, type guards and identity

Objects and arrays travel as properties, declared with `prop.value`. Its check can be a
Standard Schema or a plain type guard:

```ts
// src/seat-picker.ts
import * as v from 'valibot';
import { define, html, prop, type PropsOf, type Stateless } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Seat {
  readonly row: number;
  readonly label: string;
}

/** A type guard: the simplest check for a property. */
const isSeat = (u: unknown): u is Seat =>
  typeof u === 'object' &&
  u !== null &&
  'row' in u &&
  typeof u.row === 'number' &&
  'label' in u &&
  typeof u.label === 'string';

/** Declared once and passed by name, so production builds can leave it out. */
const Seats = v.array(v.object({ row: v.number(), label: v.string() }));

const props = {
  seats: prop.value(Seats, { default: [] }),
  chosen: prop.value(isSeat),
  /** `null` means "nobody"; leaving it unset means the default. */
  holder: prop.value(v.nullable(v.string()), { default: 'Box office' }),
};

export const SeatPicker = define<Stateless, never, PropsOf<typeof props>>()('my-seat-picker', {
  props,
  intent: {},
  update: {},
  view: (_s, _i, { props: p }) => html`
    <p>${p.seats.length} seats, held by ${p.holder ?? 'nobody'}</p>
    ${p.chosen === undefined ? '' : html`<p>Chosen: ${p.chosen.label}</p>`}
  `,
});
```

- **A type guard** `(u: unknown) => u is T` works in `prop.value()` and `prop.json()`, and the
  prop's type is its `T`. A guard that returns `false` is reported like a schema issue, with the
  guard's name.
- **A property keeps the object it was given**: after `el.seats = seats`, `el.seats === seats`.
  Development checks the value and keeps the input, not the schema's output; production skips
  the check. So a schema for a property should **check, not decode**: turning strings into
  `Date`s, filling in defaults or stripping keys would happen only to attributes, whose value is
  the parse's output.
- **Declare a schema once and pass it by name.** Production client builds never run a
  `prop.value` check, and `gyral()` removes it when it is a name (`prop.value(Seats)`,
  `schemas.seat`) or an inline function, so the schema's code can leave the bundle. A call
  written in place, such as `prop.value(v.array(Seat))`, stays, because evaluating it could have
  effects. `prop.json` keeps its check: attributes are always parsed.
- **Whether the schema really leaves is up to the bundler.** Vite 8.3 (Rolldown) keeps schema
  code in a lazily loaded chunk once the schema library sits in a chunk shared with the entry,
  even when its builders are marked free of side effects. So the saving shows in single-chunk
  builds, and for schemas whose library isn't shared across chunks.
- **`null` for an explicit "nobody".** A `default` replaces only `undefined`: setting a prop to
  `undefined`, or removing its attribute, brings the default back. Make the schema nullable and
  pass `.holder=${null}` (or the attribute `holder="null"` with `prop.json`).

### When a prop counts as changed

A write whose value equals the old one changes nothing: no render, no `PropsChanged`. That
holds for property sets and attribute changes alike, so a parent may write the same value on
every render without making the child do any work.

| Builder                       | Equal when                                                 |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------- |
| `string`, `number`, `boolean` | `Object.is(old, new)`                                      |
| `json`                        | `JSON.stringify` gives the same text (it is JSON data)     |
| `value`                       | `Object.is(old, new)`, or what its `equals` option returns |

So a parent can bind a fresh object on every render, `.range=${{ min: s.min, max: s.max }}`, to
a `prop.json` prop: the same JSON is the same value. Keys in a different order only cost an
extra render. `prop.value` holds anything, class instances and DOM nodes included, so it keeps
identity unless you say what "the same" means. `equals` receives the old and the new value,
`undefined` when unset, and `prop.json` takes it too:

```ts
// src/results-table.ts
import { define, html, prop, type PropsOf, type Stateless } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Sort {
  readonly key: string;
  readonly dir: 'asc' | 'desc';
}

const isSort = (u: unknown): u is Sort =>
  typeof u === 'object' &&
  u !== null &&
  'key' in u &&
  typeof u.key === 'string' &&
  'dir' in u &&
  (u.dir === 'asc' || u.dir === 'desc');

const isRange = (u: unknown): u is { readonly min: number; readonly max: number } =>
  typeof u === 'object' &&
  u !== null &&
  'min' in u &&
  typeof u.min === 'number' &&
  'max' in u &&
  typeof u.max === 'number';

const sortLabel = (sort: Sort): string =>
  `Sorted by ${sort.key}, ${sort.dir === 'asc' ? 'ascending' : 'descending'}`;

const props = {
  /** Compared by JSON text: a fresh but equal object changes nothing. */
  range: prop.json(isRange, { default: { min: 0, max: 100 } }),
  /** Compared field by field, instead of by identity. */
  sort: prop.value(isSort, { equals: (a, b) => a?.key === b?.key && a?.dir === b?.dir }),
};

export const ResultsTable = define<Stateless, never, PropsOf<typeof props>>()('my-results-table', {
  props,
  intent: {},
  update: {},
  view: (_s, _i, { props: p }) => html`
    <p>Prices ${p.range.min} to ${p.range.max}</p>
    ${p.sort === undefined ? '' : html`<p>${sortLabel(p.sort)}</p>`}
  `,
});
```

When no `equals` fits, keep bound objects stable in the parent instead: build them in a reducer,
so they live in state, rather than in the view, so an unchanged object is the same object.

### Reacting to prop changes

When a declared prop changes after the first render, the component receives the framework
message `PropsChanged`, with the new and previous props (a write of an [equal
value](#when-a-prop-counts-as-changed) sends nothing). Its reducer is optional. It is the only
way props enter state, so "reset when the user changes" is explicit:

```ts
// src/user-notes.ts
import { define, html, prop } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly draft: string;
}

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Typed'; readonly text: string };

export const UserNotes = define<State, Msg, { readonly userId: string }>()('my-user-notes', {
  props: { userId: prop.string({ required: true }) },
  init: () => ({ draft: '' }),
  intent: { Typed: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Typed', text: value ?? '' }) },
  update: {
    Typed: (s, m) => ({ ...s, draft: m.text }),
    // A different user: start a fresh draft.
    PropsChanged: (s, m) => (m.props.userId === m.prev.userId ? s : { draft: '' }),
  },
  view: (s, i, { props }) => html`
    <label for="notes">Note about ${props.userId}</label>
    <input id="notes" data-intent=${i.Typed} value=${s.draft} />
  `,
});
```

Like any reducer, the `PropsChanged` reducer may return commands, for example to load data for
the new user.

## Child components and outputs

A parent sets a child's props in its view, as attributes (`step="5"`) or as properties
(`.step=${5}`, the way objects and arrays travel), and listens to the child's **outputs**. A
child reports up by returning an output from a reducer, a command like any other, so the child
stays pure and testable. Build the helper once with `const emit = outputs<Out>()`, a module
constant like `intentsOf<typeof Component>()`: typed by the output union, so an output of the
wrong shape fails to compile in the child.

```ts
// src/stepper.ts
import { define, html, outputs, prop, type Stateless } from '@gyral/core';

/** What the stepper tells its parent. */
export type StepperOutput = { readonly _tag: 'Stepped'; readonly by: number };

const emit = outputs<StepperOutput>();

type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Step'; readonly by: number };

export const Stepper = define<Stateless, Msg, { readonly step: number }, StepperOutput>()(
  'my-stepper',
  {
    props: { step: prop.number({ default: 1 }) },
    intent: {
      Step: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Step', by: Number(value) }),
    },
    update: {
      Step: (s, m, { props }) => [s, [emit({ _tag: 'Stepped', by: m.by * props.step })]],
    },
    view: (_s, i, { props }) => html`
      <button type="button" value="-1" data-intent=${i.Step}>−${props.step}</button>
      <button type="button" value="1" data-intent=${i.Step}>+${props.step}</button>
    `,
  },
);
```

The fourth type parameter is the output union. The parent parses outputs as intents, with
`child()`, which types the output by the child class:

```ts
// src/total.ts
import { child, define, html } from '@gyral/core';
import { Stepper } from './stepper.js';

export interface State {
  readonly total: number;
}

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Add'; readonly by: number };

export const Total = define<State, Msg>()('my-total', {
  init: () => ({ total: 0 }),
  intent: {
    Add: child(Stepper, (out) => ({ _tag: 'Add', by: out.by })),
  },
  update: {
    Add: (s, m) => ({ total: s.total + m.by }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <my-stepper .step=${5} data-intent=${i.Add}></my-stepper>
    <p>Total: <output>${s.total}</output></p>
  `,
});
```

- Outputs are delivered as a `gyral-output` event from the child's host, and they reach only
  the direct parent: once the parent's `child()` intent takes one, it goes no further. A
  grandchild's outputs never reach the grandparent, and content slotted into a child belongs to
  the component that wrote it.
- Leave the mapper's return type off, as above. Annotating it with the whole union,
  `(out): Msg => …`, fails with a long `IntentParser<…>` error, because each intent produces its
  own variant (see [Intent](https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/#typing-parsers)).
- The mapper also receives the child element, typed with its props, which is how an item in a
  list says which item it is: `child(Item, (out, el) => ({ _tag: 'Item', id: el.itemId, out }))`.
- For lists, render children with `each(items, key, row)`. Keys keep each child, and its state,
  attached to its item when the list reorders (see [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#lists)).
- A component that contains itself (a folder tree) passes a function, `child(() => Folder, …)`,
  so the class can refer to itself.

Shadow DOM does the isolating, and `each` does the list.

### Outputs and other code

A parent that isn't a Gyral component, such as page script or an element from another library,
hears a Gyral child's outputs as events. `OUTPUT_EVENT` (`'gyral-output'`) names the event, its
`detail` is the output, and `OutputEvent<OutputsOf<typeof Child>>` types it:

```ts
// src/reviews.ts
import { OUTPUT_EVENT, type OutputEvent, type OutputsOf } from '@gyral/core';
import { Stepper } from './stepper.js';

// Listen on the child or on an ancestor in the same tree.
document.querySelector('#reviews')?.addEventListener(OUTPUT_EVENT, (event) => {
  const { detail } = event as OutputEvent<OutputsOf<typeof Stepper>>;
  console.log(`Stepped by ${String(detail.by)}`, event.target);
});
```

The event bubbles but isn't composed, so it stays in the tree the child sits in. The other
direction works too: any custom element talks to a Gyral parent by dispatching
`new CustomEvent(OUTPUT_EVENT, { detail: { _tag: 'Picked' }, bubbles: true })` on itself, so
children don't have to be Gyral components. [Using Gyral in other
frameworks](https://gyral.dev/docs/other-frameworks/#outputs-the-gyral-output-event) has recipes.

## Escape hatches

- **`el.send(msg)`** feeds a message into a component from imperative code (a canvas, an
  observer). Prefer intents and drivers where you can.
- **Any custom element.** Gyral components are plain custom elements, and any other custom
  element works alongside them, whether you wrote it by hand or with another library (see
  [Using third-party web components](https://gyral.dev/docs/third-party-components/)). Gyral adds a loop, not a
  walled garden.

---

# Intent

> How Gyral turns clicks, input, form submissions and keys into typed messages, and why the view never holds event handlers.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/

**Intent** answers one question: what did the user mean? It turns platform events into
messages, and it is the only place where raw input is read. Everything after it, the model and
the view, works with typed, already-parsed data.

Building a form with validation? The [Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/#complete-example-a-validated-form)
page starts with a complete, copyable component: the submit intent, the messages, the reducers,
focus and the error markup in one file. [Form submissions](#form-submissions) below sums it up.

```ts
// src/search-box.ts
import { define, html } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly query: string;
  readonly submitted: string | undefined;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Typed'; readonly query: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Search'; readonly query: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Clear' };

export const SearchBox = define<State, Msg>()('my-search-box', {
  init: () => ({ query: '', submitted: undefined }),
  intent: {
    Typed: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Typed', query: value ?? '' }),
    Search: ({ formData }) => {
      const q = formData?.get('q');
      return typeof q === 'string' && q.trim() !== ''
        ? { _tag: 'Search', query: q.trim() }
        : undefined;
    },
    Clear: ({ key }) => (key === 'Escape' ? { _tag: 'Clear' } : undefined),
  },
  update: {
    Typed: (s, m) => ({ ...s, query: m.query }),
    Search: (s, m) => ({ ...s, submitted: m.query }),
    Clear: () => ({ query: '', submitted: undefined }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <search data-intent=${i.Clear} data-intent-on="keydown">
      <form data-intent=${i.Search}>
        <label for="q">Search</label>
        <input id="q" name="q" type="search" value=${s.query} data-intent=${i.Typed} />
        <button>Search</button>
      </form>
    </search>
    <p>${s.submitted === undefined ? 'Nothing searched yet.' : `Results for “${s.submitted}”`}</p>
  `,
});
```

## Naming intents in markup

The view puts `data-intent=${i.Search}` on an element. `i` holds the intent names (the keys of
`intent`), typed, so a misspelt intent is a compile error. When that element's trigger event fires, Gyral calls the
parser registered under the same name in `intent`, and sends whatever it returns through
`update`.

A parser that only sends its tag can be written `true`: `intent: { Clear: true }` is
`Clear: () => ({ _tag: 'Clear' })`. It works when the message has no other fields, and is a type
error otherwise. A component with no intents leaves `intent` out, and one with no messages
leaves `update` out too.

The view never attaches a closure. That keeps it a pure function of state, which matters for
[server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/) (the markup the server sends already names every
intent) and for testing (there's nothing to call but `update`).

## Trigger events

Each element has a natural event, so you rarely say which one:

| Element                                  | Fires on                                |
| ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------- |
| `<form>`                                 | `submit` (Gyral prevents the page load) |
| `<input>` (text-like), `<textarea>`      | `input`                                 |
| checkbox and radio `<input>`, `<select>` | `change`                                |
| a custom element (a child component)     | its outputs                             |
| anything else (`<button>`, …)            | `click`                                 |

Override it with `data-intent-on`, such as `data-intent-on="keydown"`. Any event type works
there: `keyup`, `focusin`, `focusout`, `toggle` (popovers and `<details>`), `command` (invoker
commands, below), `pointerdown` or a third-party element's own event. A component listens only
for the events its templates name, so a component without keyboard intents never runs intent
lookup on a keystroke. If the value itself is bound, `data-intent-on=${…}`, the component listens
for `keydown`, `keyup`, `focusin`, `focusout`, `toggle` and `command` as well; for any other
event, write a per-event attribute such as `data-intent-pointerdown=${i.Press}` (below), which
the component always listens for.

`data-intent-on` also takes a list, separated by spaces: `data-intent-on="keydown keyup"` fires
the intent for both events. The parser tells them apart with `event.type`. Use a list when the
events mean the same thing to the model, such as the press and the release of a
[hold-to-record button](#press-and-hold).

## One element, an intent per event

When each event on an element means something different, name an intent per event type with
`data-intent-<event>`. A task in a sortable list grabs on `pointerdown`, drops on `pointerup`,
moves with the keyboard and tracks focus, all on the `<li>` itself:

```ts
// src/task-list.ts
import { define, each, html, intentsOf, on, type TemplateResult } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Task {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly title: string;
}

export interface State {
  readonly tasks: readonly Task[];
  readonly dragging: string | undefined;
  readonly focused: string | undefined;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Grab'; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Drop'; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Move'; readonly id: string; readonly by: -1 | 1 }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Focus'; readonly id: string };

// The component's intent names, for rows. A row's return type is written out, or the row and
// `TaskList`'s type would infer each other.
const i = intentsOf<typeof TaskList>();

const TaskRow = (t: Task): TemplateResult =>
  html`<li
    tabindex="0"
    data-id=${t.id}
    data-intent-pointerdown=${i.Grab}
    data-intent-pointerup=${i.Drop}
    data-intent-keydown=${i.Move}
    data-intent-focusin=${i.Focus}
  >
    ${t.title}
  </li>`;

const idOf = (el: Element): string => el.getAttribute('data-id') ?? '';

/** Moves the task `id` to the place `to(from)` gives, clamped to the list. */
const moved = (tasks: readonly Task[], id: string, to: (from: number) => number) => {
  const from = tasks.findIndex((t) => t.id === id);
  const task = tasks[from];
  if (task === undefined) return tasks;
  const rest = tasks.filter((t) => t !== task);
  const at = Math.max(0, Math.min(rest.length, to(from)));
  return [...rest.slice(0, at), task, ...rest.slice(at)];
};

export const TaskList = define<State, Msg>()('my-task-list', {
  init: () => ({
    tasks: [
      { id: 'a', title: 'Write the brief' },
      { id: 'b', title: 'Review the designs' },
    ],
    dragging: undefined,
    focused: undefined,
  }),
  intent: {
    Grab: ({ target }) => ({ _tag: 'Grab', id: idOf(target) }),
    // Released over another task: the dragged one moves there.
    Drop: ({ target }) => ({ _tag: 'Drop', id: idOf(target) }),
    // Alt+ArrowUp and Alt+ArrowDown move the focused task; other keys keep their default.
    Move: on('keydown', { keys: ['ArrowUp', 'ArrowDown'], modifiers: { alt: true } }, (input) => {
      input.event.preventDefault();
      return { _tag: 'Move', id: idOf(input.target), by: input.key === 'ArrowUp' ? -1 : 1 };
    }),
    Focus: ({ target }) => ({ _tag: 'Focus', id: idOf(target) }),
  },
  update: {
    Grab: (s, m) => ({ ...s, dragging: m.id }),
    Drop: (s, m) => {
      const onto = s.tasks.findIndex((t) => t.id === m.id);
      return s.dragging === undefined
        ? s
        : { ...s, dragging: undefined, tasks: moved(s.tasks, s.dragging, () => onto) };
    },
    Move: (s, m) => ({ ...s, tasks: moved(s.tasks, m.id, (from) => from + m.by) }),
    Focus: (s, m) => ({ ...s, focused: m.id }),
  },
  view: (s) => html`
    <ul aria-label="Tasks">
      ${each(s.tasks, (t) => t.id, TaskRow)}
    </ul>
  `,
});
```

- **Per-event attributes come first.** For an event of type T, an element's `data-intent-T`
  answers before its plain `data-intent`, which keeps handling its own trigger. Lookup still
  starts at the element that was hit and goes outward, and the nearest element with an intent
  for that event wins.
- **Write the event name in lower case**, as event types are: `data-intent-pointerdown`. The HTML
  parser lower-cases attribute names, so an event whose name has capitals, such as a library's
  `valueChange`, can't be named this way: `data-intent-valueChange` becomes
  `data-intent-valuechange`. Put such a name in `data-intent-on` instead.
- **`data-intent-on` is reserved** for the trigger list. It is never read as an event called
  `on`.
- **The component listens for every event these names mention**, bound or static, in list rows
  and in `raw()` markup too. No `events` entry is needed.
- `data-intent-keydown=${s.editing ? i.Key : nothing}` gives the element that intent only while
  editing.

When the events share one message, keep one `data-intent` with a `data-intent-on` list instead.
And an intent can still sit on an ancestor, as `Clear` does in the first example: keys typed in
the input bubble to the `<search>` around it. `data-intent-keydown=${i.Clear}` on the input
itself would work as well.

## What a parser receives

A parser gets an `IntentInput` object, and the component's read-only context as a second
argument (see [props, state and stores in a parser](#props-state-and-stores-in-a-parser)):

| Field      | Holds                                                                          |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `value`    | The `value` of the input, select, textarea or button that has the intent       |
| `checked`  | `checked`, for checkboxes and radios                                           |
| `formData` | The submitted `FormData` (with the submitter button), for a `<form>`           |
| `key`      | `KeyboardEvent.key`, for `keydown` and `keyup`                                 |
| `newState` | `'open'` or `'closed'`, for `toggle`                                           |
| `detail`   | The `detail` of any `CustomEvent`: a child's output, a library element's event |
| `command`  | The invoker command and its source, for `command`                              |
| `name`     | The intent's name: the `data-intent-<event>` or `data-intent` value            |
| `event`    | The raw event                                                                  |
| `target`   | The element that carries the intent                                            |

Prefer the parsed fields to `event`: they read the same way for every element, and they're
what [tests](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/) can construct.

### The intent element and the element that was hit

Read the element with the intent from `target`, not from the event. Gyral listens on the
component's root, so `event.currentTarget` is that root (the shadow root, or the host of a
light-DOM component), and `event.target` is whatever was hit inside the element: the `<span>`
in a button's label, an icon. `target` is always the element whose intent attribute answered.
Compare the two when it matters where an event started, as in
[declining](#declining-passing-an-event-outward).

`detail` is `unknown` until the parser checks it, with a type guard or a schema, because any
element can dispatch a `CustomEvent`. [Using third-party web
components](https://gyral.dev/docs/third-party-components/#what-the-parser-gets) shows a map's custom event
parsed this way.

### Parsers typed by their event

`on(event, [filter], parser)` from `@gyral/core` is a parser for one event type. Its input is
typed by that event, so `input.event` is a `KeyboardEvent` for `keydown`, a `DragEvent` for
`drop` and a `SubmitEvent` for `submit`, and it adds what parsers otherwise dig out of the event
themselves:

| Field           | Holds                                                                                  |
| --------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `control`       | The `input`, `select`, `textarea` or `button` that has the intent, typed               |
| `form`          | That control's form, or the `<form>` that has the intent                               |
| `modifiers`     | `{ shift, ctrl, alt, meta }`, all `false` for events without modifier keys             |
| `files`         | The files from a file input, a drop or a paste; `undefined` for other events           |
| `valueAsNumber` | A number, range, date or time input's value as a number; `undefined` when it's invalid |
| `origin`        | The element the event started on (`composedPath()[0]`), inside shadow roots too        |

A key filter, `{ keys, modifiers }`, declines other keys the way returning `undefined` does:
they pass outward and keep their default action, so Ctrl+R still reloads the page. `modifiers`
is `'none'`, `'any'`, or the keys that must be held or not, such as `{ ctrl: true }`:

```ts
// src/board.ts
import { define, html, on } from '@gyral/core';

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Move'; readonly by: -1 | 1 }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Attach'; readonly files: readonly File[] }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Volume'; readonly level: number };

export const Board = define<{ readonly at: number }, Msg>()('my-board', {
  init: () => ({ at: 0 }),
  intent: {
    // Only the two arrows, with no modifier held: Alt+ArrowLeft still goes back.
    Move: on('keydown', { keys: ['ArrowLeft', 'ArrowRight'], modifiers: 'none' }, (input) => ({
      _tag: 'Move',
      by: input.key === 'ArrowLeft' ? -1 : 1,
    })),
    Attach: on('change', (input) => ({ _tag: 'Attach', files: input.files ?? [] })),
    Volume: on('input', (input) =>
      input.valueAsNumber === undefined
        ? undefined
        : { _tag: 'Volume', level: input.valueAsNumber },
    ),
  },
  update: {
    Move: (s, m) => ({ at: s.at + m.by }),
    Attach: (s) => s,
    Volume: (s) => s,
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <p tabindex="0" data-intent-keydown=${i.Move}>Position: ${s.at}</p>
    <label>Attachments <input type="file" multiple data-intent-change=${i.Attach} /></label>
    <label>Volume <input type="range" data-intent-input=${i.Volume} /></label>
  `,
});
```

Bind the intent to the parser's event, with `data-intent-<event>` or `data-intent-on`, or rely on
the element's own trigger. In development, a parser that another event reaches throws
([G0018](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0018)), and the `gyral/intent-event` lint rule reports such a binding in your
editor. Plain parsers keep `IntentInput`, and `on()` is a module of its own: an app that never
calls it doesn't bundle it.

## Parse, don't validate

A parser returns one of three things:

- **A message** of its own tag's variant.
- **`undefined`** to decline the event. Above, `Clear` declines every key but Escape, and
  `Search` declines an empty query. Declining is not an error, and an intent further out may
  still take the event ([below](#declining-passing-an-event-outward)).
- **`IntentRejected`**, a framework message with field issues, when input fails a schema. The
  [Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/) helpers `form()` and `field()` produce it for you.

Parsers may return a promise, because schema validation can be async. They must not do side
effects. The one exception is `event.preventDefault()`, for example to stop arrow keys moving
the caret.

## Form submissions
