with no inline style at all. Continuous values go in custom properties with a fallback in the
stylesheet, such as `inline-size: var(--sidebar, 16rem)`: the first paint uses the fallback,
and the user's width arrives with hydration. A page rendered per request can also allow its own
style attributes by hash, with `renderPage({ csp: { styleAttributes: 'hash' } })`
([Server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/#content-security-policy)), so they paint before
hydration.

## Custom states

To style by what the model says, mirror boolean facts onto the element's custom states with
`states`. CSS then reads them with `:state()`, inside and outside the component:

```ts
// src/upload.ts
import { css, define, html } from '@gyral/core';

export interface State {
  readonly phase: 'idle' | 'uploading' | 'failed';
}

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Retry' };

export const Upload = define<State, Msg>()('my-upload', {
  init: () => ({ phase: 'idle' }),
  intent: { Retry: () => ({ _tag: 'Retry' }) },
  update: { Retry: () => ({ phase: 'uploading' }) },
  states: (s) => ({ busy: s.phase === 'uploading', failed: s.phase === 'failed' }),
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <p aria-busy=${s.phase === 'uploading'}>${s.phase}</p>
    <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Retry}>Retry</button>
  `,
  styles: css`
    :host(:state(failed)) p {
      color: var(--danger, crimson);
    }
  `,
});
```

From the page: `my-upload:state(busy) { opacity: 0.6; }`. No classes to keep in sync, and the
model stays the single source of truth. Custom states are for styling; accessibility state still
belongs in ARIA attributes such as `aria-busy`, as above. They are applied in the browser only.

## Cascade layers

Put every stylesheet in a layer, and declare the order once:

```css
@layer reset, tokens, base, components, theme;
```

Later layers win regardless of specificity, so a theme never has to out-specify a component.
Gyral's examples and the [gyral-shop](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral-shop) put component CSS
in `@layer component` (or `components`) and leave the last layer for themes.

## Light-DOM components

Some components are pages, not widgets: a product listing with its `<h1>`, a docs article. For
those, `shadow: false` renders the view as the element's own children:

```ts
// src/article-page.ts
import { define, html, prop, type Stateless } from '@gyral/core';

export const ArticlePage = define<Stateless, never, { readonly heading: string }>()(
  'my-article-page',
  {
    shadow: false,
    props: { heading: prop.string({ required: true }) },
    intent: {},
    update: {},
    view: (_s, _i, { props }) => html`
      <article>
        <h1>${props.heading}</h1>
      </article>
    `,
  },
);
```

- Document CSS applies directly, so the page's stylesheet and theme can lay it out.
- On the server it renders as plain HTML, with no `<template shadowrootmode>`, which every
  crawler and reader mode understands.
- It has no `styles` and no `<slot>`s: it owns all its children. Don't write children inside
  its tag in a template; pass data as props (the server throws on children it would have to
  drop). Scope its CSS with `@scope (my-article-page) { … }` or by tag name.
- Children in the page's HTML are fallback content, shown without JavaScript: its first render
  in the browser replaces them, as a shadow root's does. A server-rendered one keeps the
  server's children and hydrates them in place.
- Intent isolation still holds: a light component's intents stop at the next Gyral component
  inside it.

Keep widgets (buttons, dialogs, form controls) in Shadow DOM, and use light DOM for page
structure.

## A whole site as a theme

Put those together and a site's look can live entirely in CSS, the way the
[CSS Zen Garden](https://csszengarden.com) did it. gyral-shop's theme contract is a worked
example:

1. **Markup is semantic and theme-neutral.** Elements are chosen for meaning, never for looks.
2. **Stable hooks.** Pages carry `data-region="listing"`, components `data-component="price"`,
   and regions and cards declare container names. Hooks are documented, and renaming one is a
   breaking change.
3. **Tokens.** Every colour, font, radius, spacing and motion value is a custom property, set
   for light and dark with `light-dark()`. A check in the build rejects literal colours outside
   token files.
4. **Light DOM for page structure, Shadow DOM for widgets.** Themes can re-lay out pages with
   grid areas, container queries and `:has()`, and restyle widgets through tokens and parts.
5. **Themes are stylesheets** in `@layer theme`. The server renders the chosen theme's
   `<link>`, so there's no flash of the wrong theme.

The shop switches between four themes this way, from a dense marketplace to an airy boutique,
without changing any markup. See them on the [home page](https://gyral.dev/#showcase).

---

# Forms

> A complete validated form to copy, then the browser's own checks or one Standard Schema for client and server. Works with or without JavaScript.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/

Gyral forms are real `<form>` elements, and a submit is an intent like any other. Start from
the complete example below: one component with everything a validated form needs, built on the
browser's own checks, with no extra packages. Copy it and change the fields; you don't need
another page to make it work.

## Complete example: a validated form

A signup form with a name, an email, a password and a checkbox the user must tick. On submit it
shows every error next to its field, announces how many fields to fix, and moves focus to the
first invalid one. Fixing a field clears its error; a valid submit announces a welcome.

```ts
// src/account-form.ts
import { define, focus, html } from '@gyral/core';

/** The fields, in the order they appear: the first one with an error gets focus. */
export const FIELDS = ['name', 'email', 'password', 'consent'] as const;
export type Field = (typeof FIELDS)[number];

/** One message per field; `''` means no error. */
export type Errors = Readonly<Record<Field, string>>;

export const NO_ERRORS: Errors = { name: '', email: '', password: '', consent: '' };

export interface State {
  readonly errors: Errors;
  /** What the live region announces after a rejected submit; `''` otherwise. */
  readonly summary: string;
  /** The clean values after a successful signup. */
  readonly account: { readonly name: string; readonly email: string } | undefined;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Rejected'; readonly errors: Errors }
  | { readonly _tag: 'SignedUp'; readonly name: string; readonly email: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Checked'; readonly field: Field; readonly error: string };

const isField = (name: string): name is Field => FIELDS.some((f) => f === name);

/**
 * Your message for a field's first problem, from the browser's own checks (`validity`), or
 * `''` when the field is fine. The constraints in the markup (`required`, `type="email"`,
 * `minlength`) still decide what is wrong; `novalidate` only stops the browser from
 * blocking the submit and showing its own bubble.
 */
export function problemWith(input: HTMLInputElement): string {
  const { validity } = input;
  // A checkbox is missing when unchecked. `required` accepts "   ", so blank text is missing too.
  const missing =
    input.type === 'checkbox' ? !input.checked : validity.valueMissing || input.value.trim() === '';
  switch (input.name) {
    case 'name':
      return missing ? 'Enter your name.' : '';
    case 'email':
      if (missing) return 'Enter your email address.';
      return validity.typeMismatch ? 'Enter an email address like ada@example.com.' : '';
    case 'password':
      if (missing) return 'Enter a password.';
      // `tooShort` is set only for typed values; the length check also covers a pre-filled one.
      return validity.tooShort || input.value.length < input.minLength
        ? 'Use at least 8 characters.'
        : '';
    case 'consent':
      return missing ? 'Accept the privacy policy to continue.' : '';
    default:
      return '';
  }
}

/** What the status region announces after a successful signup. */
const welcome = (account: State['account']): string =>
  account === undefined ? '' : `Welcome, ${account.name}! We’ll write to ${account.email}.`;

/** Reads a submitted form: every field's error, or the clean values. */
function submission(form: Element, data: FormData | undefined): Msg | undefined {
  if (!(form instanceof HTMLFormElement) || data === undefined) return undefined;
  const errors: Record<Field, string> = { ...NO_ERRORS };
  for (const field of FIELDS) {
    const input = form.elements.namedItem(field);
    if (input instanceof HTMLInputElement) errors[field] = problemWith(input);
  }
  if (FIELDS.some((f) => errors[f] !== '')) return { _tag: 'Rejected', errors };
  const text = (field: Field): string => {
    const value = data.get(field);
    return typeof value === 'string' ? value.trim() : '';
  };
  // The password stays in the form data: never keep it in state.
  return { _tag: 'SignedUp', name: text('name'), email: text('email') };
}

export const AccountForm = define<State, Msg>()('my-account-form', {
  init: () => ({ errors: NO_ERRORS, summary: '', account: undefined }),
  intent: {
    // Not a message tag, so it may return either message.
    Submit: ({ target, formData }) => submission(target, formData),
    // Text fields send it on `input`, the checkbox on `change`.
    Checked: ({ target }) =>
      target instanceof HTMLInputElement && isField(target.name)
        ? { _tag: 'Checked', field: target.name, error: problemWith(target) }
        : undefined,
  },
  update: {
    // Show every error at once, announce how many, and focus the first field that has one.
    Rejected: (s, m) => {
      const count = FIELDS.filter((f) => m.errors[f] !== '').length;
      const first = FIELDS.find((f) => m.errors[f] !== '');
      const summary = `Fix ${String(count)} ${count === 1 ? 'field' : 'fields'} to continue.`;
      const focusFirst = first === undefined ? [] : [focus(`#${first}`)];
      return [{ ...s, errors: m.errors, summary }, focusFirst];
    },
    // In an app, this also returns the command that posts the form.
    SignedUp: (_s, m) => ({
      errors: NO_ERRORS,
      summary: '',
      account: { name: m.name, email: m.email },
    }),
    // While the user types, only a field that already shows an error is checked again,
    // so a message changes or disappears as soon as the value is fixed.
    Checked: (s, m) =>
      s.errors[m.field] === '' ? s : { ...s, errors: { ...s.errors, [m.field]: m.error } },
  },
  // No `value` bindings: what the user typed stays in the fields after a rejected submit.
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <form novalidate data-intent=${i.Submit}>
      <p role="alert">${s.summary}</p>

      <label for="name">Name</label>
      <input
        id="name"
        name="name"
        autocomplete="name"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.name !== ''}
        aria-describedby="name-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="name-error">${s.errors.name}</p>

      <label for="email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        autocomplete="email"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.email !== ''}
        aria-describedby="email-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="email-error">${s.errors.email}</p>

      <label for="password">Password</label>
      <input
        id="password"
        name="password"
        type="password"
        autocomplete="new-password"
        required
        minlength="8"
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.password !== ''}
        aria-describedby="password-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <p id="password-error">${s.errors.password}</p>

      <input
        id="consent"
        name="consent"
        type="checkbox"
        required
        aria-invalid=${s.errors.consent !== ''}
        aria-describedby="consent-error"
        data-intent=${i.Checked}
      />
      <label for="consent">I accept the privacy policy</label>
      <p id="consent-error">${s.errors.consent}</p>

      <button>Create account</button>
    </form>
    <p role="status">${welcome(s.account)}</p>
  `,
});
```

What each part does:

- **`novalidate` on the form, constraints on the fields.** `required`, `type="email"` and
  `minlength` still set each field's `validity`; `novalidate` only stops the browser from
  blocking the submit with its own bubble. Without it, no `submit` event fires and your
  messages never appear.
- **The submit intent is the parser.** `data-intent=${i.Submit}` on the `<form>` runs `Submit`
  on `submit` (and Gyral prevents the page load). `target` is the `<form>`, so
  `target.elements.namedItem('email')` is the email input, and `formData` holds the submitted
  values. `Submit` isn't a message tag, so it may return either message: `Rejected` with every
  field's error, or `SignedUp` with the trimmed values.
- **`problemWith(input)` turns `validity` into your words**: `valueMissing`, `typeMismatch`,
  `tooShort`, and `checked` for the checkbox. It trims first, because `required` accepts a value
  of spaces.
- **Errors are state**: one string per field, `''` for none. The view writes each message in a
  `<p>` next to its field, links it with `aria-describedby` and sets `aria-invalid`.
- **The `role="alert"` paragraph announces the summary.** It is always rendered, empty until a
  submit fails, so screen readers announce the text when it appears. `role="status"` announces
  the welcome the same way, politely.
- **Focus moves to the first invalid field** with a `focus()` command returned from the
  `Rejected` reducer. Commands are data; the runtime moves the focus after rendering.
- **Fixing a field clears its error.** Each control sends `Checked` (text fields on `input`,
  the checkbox on `change`); the reducer updates only a field that already shows an error, so
  nothing turns red while someone is still typing.
- **Values stay in the fields.** The view binds no `value`, so a rejected submit leaves what the
  user typed. Bind `value=${s.name}` only when state must set the text, such as emptying a
  field after a submit.
- **Enter submits**, because the form has a submit button, and a click submits the same way.
- **No password in state.** `SignedUp` carries the name and the email only.

To adapt it, add the field's name to `FIELDS`, give it a `case` in `problemWith`, and render a
labelled control with the same `id` and `name` plus its error `<p>`. To send the form to a
server, keep the raw `FormData` in the message and return a command that posts it, as in
[Submitting to the server](#submitting-to-the-server). The
[signup form recipe](https://gyral.dev/docs/recipes/#a-signup-form-with-native-validation) has the same
component with its tests: the reducers without a browser, and the parser with `mount()`.

There are two ways to validate a form. The example uses the first; add the second when a server
needs the same rules.

- **[Native validation](#native-validation)**, with no extra packages. The browser's
  constraints (`required`, `type="email"`, `minlength`) find what is wrong, and the submit
  parser reads each field's `validity` and returns your messages. It works in any app,
  including a new `basic` one.
- **[One schema for both sides](#one-schema-for-both-sides).** A
  [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) library validates in the browser and on the
  server, the form posts with `@gyral/http`, and the same errors render without JavaScript.

## Native validation

**`required` without `novalidate` hides your errors.** The browser checks constraints before
it fires `submit`. When one fails, it shows its own bubble and fires no `submit` event, so your
parser never runs and your messages never appear. Put `novalidate` on any form that shows its
own errors, and keep the constraints on the fields: they still set `validity`, which the parser
reads, as in the [complete example](#complete-example-a-validated-form).

Each constraint sets one `validity` flag, so the parser can say exactly what is wrong:

| Constraint                       | Flag                                              | Notes                               |
| -------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `required`                       | `valueMissing`                                    | A value of spaces passes: trim it   |
| `required` on a checkbox         | `valueMissing`                                    | Set while it is unchecked           |
| `type="email"`, `type="url"`     | `typeMismatch`                                    | Only for a value that isn't empty   |
| `minlength`, `maxlength`         | `tooShort`, `tooLong`                             | Only after the user edits the value |
| `pattern`                        | `patternMismatch`                                 |                                     |
| `min`, `max`, `step`             | `rangeUnderflow`, `rangeOverflow`, `stepMismatch` | Numbers, dates and times            |
| `type="number"`, unparsable text | `badInput`                                        | The `value` reads as `''`           |

`validity.valid` is `true` when no flag is set, and `form.checkValidity()` asks every field at
once. A message set with `setCustomValidity()`, as the [`invalid()`](#form-and-invalid) hook
does, sets `customError`, so read the specific flags rather than `valid` when you combine them.

`novalidate` in server-rendered markup turns validation off for visitors without JavaScript
too. If your form also posts to a server, render `?novalidate=${s.live}` and set `live` in the
`Hydrated` reducer, as in [Schema messages for everything](#schema-messages-for-everything),
and validate again on the server.

## One schema for both sides

When a server handles the form too, validate it with one schema on both sides. Each layer is
optional; use as many as a form needs:

1. **Native constraints**: `required`, `type="email"`, `minlength`, `pattern`.
2. **A schema-parsed intent**: `form(schema, toMsg)` validates the submission.
3. **Errors in the model**, mirrored into native validity with `invalid()`.
4. **Server checks** as ordinary commands: `submitForm()` posts the form.
5. **No-JavaScript parity**: the server's `formAction()` validates with the same schema and
   renders the same errors.

This path needs `@gyral/http` for the post, `@gyral/ssr` for the server half and a schema
library. Define the form once with any [Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) library, such as
Zod, Valibot, ArkType or Effect Schema. Form values arrive as strings; the schema coerces them.

```ts
// src/signup-form.ts
import { defineForm } from '@gyral/core';
import * as v from 'valibot';

export const SignupForm = defineForm(
  v.object({
    email: v.pipe(v.string(), v.trim(), v.email('Enter an email address like ada@example.com.')),
    password: v.pipe(v.string(), v.minLength(8, 'Use at least 8 characters.')),
    invite: v.optional(v.string()),
  }),
  // Never echoed back after a failed submit. Fields named like `password` are secret already.
  { secret: ['invite'] },
);
```

The definition is also what the server uses: `SignupForm.validate(data)` checks a `FormData`
the way `form()` does, and `SignupForm.values(data)` returns the submitted values to re-fill a
form, without its secret fields.

**Secret fields are never echoed.** After a failed submit, the submitted values come back so the
form can be re-filled, except fields listed in `secret` (any posted field name, not only the
schema's) and any field whose name contains `password`, `passcode`, `csrf` or `xsrf`. They're left out of `IntentRejected.values` on both paths and out of
`values()`, and the devtools timeline shows them as `[secret]`. Development builds warn once
about an unlisted field whose name looks secret (`token`, `card`, `cvc`, …).

## form() and invalid()

```ts
// src/signup.ts
import { define, fieldErrors, form, html, invalid } from '@gyral/core';
import { redirectedTo, submitForm } from '@gyral/http';
import { SignupForm } from './signup-form.js';

export interface State {
  readonly email: string;
  readonly errors: Readonly<Record<string, readonly string[]>>;
  readonly busy: boolean;
  readonly done: string | undefined;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Submit'; readonly form: FormData }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Done'; readonly location: string | undefined }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed' };

export const Signup = define<State, Msg>()('my-signup', {
  init: () => ({ email: '', errors: {}, busy: false, done: undefined }),
  intent: {
    // Valid in the browser: post the raw FormData so the server parses it like a no-JS post.
    Submit: form(SignupForm, (_data, raw) => ({ _tag: 'Submit', form: raw })),
  },
  update: {
    Submit: (s, m) => [
      { ...s, errors: {}, busy: true },
      [
        submitForm('/signup', m.form, {
          onSuccess: (body): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Done', location: redirectedTo(body) }),
          onFailure: (): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Failed' }),
        }),
      ],
    ],
    Done: (s, m) => ({ ...s, busy: false, done: m.location ?? '/' }),
    Failed: (s) => ({ ...s, busy: false, errors: { '': ['Something went wrong. Try again.'] } }),
    // Browser-side and server-side rejections arrive as the same message.
    IntentRejected: (s, m) => ({
      ...s,
      busy: false,
      email: typeof m.values?.['email'] === 'string' ? m.values['email'] : s.email,
      errors: fieldErrors(m.issues),
    }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <form data-intent=${i.Submit} action="/signup" method="post">
      <label for="email">Email</label>
      <input
        id="email"
        name="email"
        type="email"
        autocomplete="email"
        required
        value=${s.email}
        aria-describedby="email-error"
        ${invalid(s.errors['email'])}
      />
      <span id="email-error">${s.errors['email']?.join(' ') ?? ''}</span>

      <label for="password">Password</label>
      <input
        id="password"
        name="password"
        type="password"
        autocomplete="new-password"
        minlength="8"
        required
        aria-describedby="password-error"
        ${invalid(s.errors['password'])}
      />
      <span id="password-error">${s.errors['password']?.join(' ') ?? ''}</span>

      <p role="alert">${s.errors['']?.join(' ') ?? ''}</p>
      <button ?disabled=${s.busy}>Create account</button>
    </form>
  `,
});
```

What happens on submit:

- **The browser checks native constraints first.** If `required` or `type="email"` fails, the
  browser shows its own message and no `submit` event fires, so `form()` doesn't run. Keep
  them: they work without JavaScript and are accessible. To show the schema's messages instead,
  see [Schema messages for everything](#schema-messages-for-everything).
- **`form(schema, toMsg)`** turns the `FormData` into a plain object (repeated names become
  arrays) and validates it. Valid data goes to `toMsg`, which also gets the raw `FormData`.
  Invalid data becomes `IntentRejected`, with one issue per field: `path` matches the field's
  `name`.
- **Errors live in state.** `fieldErrors(issues)` groups them by field. Keep the result in
  state: it is data, so tests can see it.
- **`invalid(errors)`** is an [element hook](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#element-hooks) that mirrors a field's
  errors into native validity: it calls `setCustomValidity` and sets `aria-invalid`, so
  `:user-invalid` styling, the browser's error bubble and your model agree. It clears the error
  when the user edits the field.
- **The server writes `aria-invalid="true"` too**: the hook has a server half that adds it to the
  rendered start tag, so the no-JavaScript page announces errors. `aria-describedby` points at
  the message, which is plain text in the view.

`field(schema, toMsg)` does the same for a single control. Pair it with
`data-intent-on="input"` to check while the user types.

## Submitting to the server

Some checks only the server can make: the email is taken, the password is wrong. That's why
the `Submit` reducer above posts the submission with `submitForm(url, formData, handlers)` from
`@gyral/http`, once it passed the browser's checks:

- The body is the `FormData` itself, so the server parses it exactly like a no-JS post.
- A `422` answer with an `IntentRejected` body goes to your `IntentRejected` reducer, the same
  one that handles browser-side rejections.
- The CSRF token comes from the `http` driver's headers, set once for the app:
  `makeHttpDriver({ headers: csrfFromMeta('csrf-token') })` ([Effects](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/)).
  `csrf: { token }` sends a token the app already holds.
- The default concurrency is `exhaust`: a double click doesn't submit twice.
- `redirectedTo(body)` reads the location when the server answered with a redirect.

## The server half

On the server, `formAction(definition, handlers)` from `@gyral/ssr` handles the same route for
both paths:

```ts
// server/app.ts
import { Hono } from 'hono';
import { html, type IntentRejected } from '@gyral/core';
import { formAction, rejectWith, renderPage, seeOther } from '@gyral/ssr';
import { SignupForm } from '../src/signup-form.js';

const taken = new Set(['ada@example.com']);

const signupPage = (rejected: IntentRejected | undefined, status = 200): Response =>
  renderPage(
    {
      title: 'Create an account',
      body: html`<main>
        <h1>Create an account</h1>
        <my-signup .initialMessages=${rejected === undefined ? [] : [rejected]}></my-signup>
      </main>`,
      scripts: ['/src/entry-client.ts'],
    },
    { status },
  );

export const app = new Hono();

app.get('/signup', () => signupPage(undefined));

app.post('/signup', (c) =>
  formAction(SignupForm, {
    intent: 'Submit', // the form's data-intent name
    valid: (data) =>
      taken.has(data.email)
        ? rejectWith([{ path: 'email', message: 'That email is already registered.' }])
        : seeOther('/welcome'),
    invalid: (rejected) => signupPage(rejected, 422),
  })(c.req.raw),
);
```

- **One validator.** `formAction` runs the definition's `validate`, as `form()` does, so a
  submission is rejected with identical issues on either path.
- **One reducer.** On failure, the server renders the component with
  `initialMessages: [rejected]`. The component's own `IntentRejected` reducer builds the error
  state during the server render, and the browser resumes from it.
- **Post/Redirect/Get.** `seeOther(url)` answers `303`, so reloading never resubmits.
- **JSON for the JavaScript path.** When `submitForm` asks for JSON, a redirect becomes
  `{ _tag: 'Redirected', location }` and a rejection a `422` without the submitted values.
  Browser form posts get HTML. Leave `invalid` out and every rejection is that JSON `422`;
  `wantsJson(request)` tells your own routes which kind of request they got.
- **`rejectWith(issues | message)`** rejects a schema-valid submission; a string is a
  form-level message (path `''`).

Never keep passwords in state either: server-rendered state is written into the page.

## Schema messages for everything

Native constraints run before `form()`, so a missing required field shows the browser's wording,
not your schema's. That's usually what you want. If you'd rather show the schema's messages for
everything, keep the constraints in the server-rendered markup and add `novalidate` once the
component is live:

```html
<form data-intent="${i.Submit}" ?novalidate="${s.live}">…</form>
```

with `Hydrated: (s) => ({ ...s, live: true })` in `update`. No-JavaScript visitors still get
native validation, and every JavaScript submit reaches `form()`.

## File uploads

For a custom element that submits a native form value, see
[Custom form controls](https://gyral.dev/docs/form-associated/).

Use a native file input and keep the raw `FormData` from the parsed submit. This sends the
file bytes instead of converting them to JSON:

```ts
// src/photo-upload.ts
import { define, defineForm, form, html } from '@gyral/core';
import { submitForm } from '@gyral/http';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const PhotoForm = defineForm(v.object({ photo: v.instance(File) }));
type State = { readonly status: string };
type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Submit'; readonly data: FormData }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Uploaded' }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed' };

export const PhotoUpload = define<State, Msg>()('photo-upload', {
  init: () => ({ status: 'Choose a photo.' }),
  intent: { Submit: form(PhotoForm, (_data, raw) => ({ _tag: 'Submit', data: raw })) },
  update: {
    Submit: (_s, m) => [
      { status: 'Uploading…' },
      [
        submitForm('/photos', m.data, {
          onSuccess: (): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Uploaded' }),
          onFailure: (): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Failed' }),
        }),
      ],
    ],
    Uploaded: () => ({ status: 'Photo uploaded.' }),
    Failed: () => ({ status: 'Upload failed. Try again.' }),
    IntentRejected: () => ({ status: 'Choose a photo before uploading.' }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <form action="/photos" method="post" enctype="multipart/form-data" data-intent=${i.Submit}>
      <label for="photo">Photo</label>
      <input id="photo" name="photo" type="file" accept="image/*" required />
      <button type="submit">Upload</button>
      <output aria-live="polite">${s.status}</output>
    </form>
  `,
});
```

Do not set `content-type` yourself: the browser adds the multipart boundary. `accept` is a
picker hint, not server validation. The server must enforce size, count, content and storage
rules and apply authentication/CSRF checks. The schema above checks only that a file object
exists; add your application's browser checks and validate again on the server. File inputs
cannot be restored from a hydration seed or sticky rejected values; keep files in the submit
boundary, not model state. See [Security](https://gyral.dev/docs/security/#uploaded-files).

---

# Custom form controls

> Make a Gyral component participate in native forms, with reset, disabled state, validity and a server-rendered fallback.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/form-associated/

Use `formAssociated` when the custom element itself should submit a native form value under
its `name` attribute. The projection stays pure; Gyral owns the ElementInternals attachment.

```ts
// src/choice-field.ts
import { define, html } from '@gyral/core';

interface State {
  readonly value: string;
  readonly live: boolean;
  readonly disabled: boolean;
}
type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Edited'; readonly value: string };

export const ChoiceField = define<State, Msg>()('my-choice-field', {
  init: () => ({ value: 'Default', live: false, disabled: false }),
  intent: { Edited: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Edited', value: value ?? '' }) },
  update: {
    Edited: (s, m) => ({ ...s, value: m.value, live: true }),
    FormDisabled: (s, m) => ({ ...s, disabled: m.disabled }),
    FormReset: (s) => ({ ...s, value: 'Default' }),
    FormStateRestore: (s, m) =>
      typeof m.state === 'string' ? { ...s, value: m.state, live: true } : s,
  },
  formAssociated: { value: (s) => (s.live ? s.value : null) },
  shadow: false,
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <label>
      Choice
      <input
        name=${s.live ? undefined : 'choice'}
        value=${s.value}
        ?disabled=${s.disabled}
        data-intent=${i.Edited}
      />
    </label>
  `,
});
```

```html
<form action="/choices" method="post">
  <my-choice-field name="choice"></my-choice-field>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
  <button type="reset">Reset</button>
</form>
```

The light DOM fallback input participates in the outer form before JavaScript runs. The
custom control returns `null` until an input event captures the live value in the model.
It then submits that value and removes the fallback's `name`, avoiding duplicate entries.
The input remains usable. Switching solely on `Hydrated` can lose a value typed before
hydration; Gyral does not automatically read arbitrary fallback inputs into state.

`value` may return a string, File, FormData or null. An optional `state` projection supplies
a separate restoration value. Keep server-rendered model state JSON-compatible; binary
values belong at the browser boundary.

An optional `validity` projection returns native flags, a message and an anchor selector:

```ts
const validity = (s: { readonly value: string }) =>
  s.value === ''
    ? { flags: { customError: true }, message: 'Enter a choice.', anchor: 'input' }
    : undefined;
```

Returning `undefined` clears validity. Mirror effective disabled state to inner controls.
`FormReset`, `FormDisabled` and `FormStateRestore` reducers are optional; reset does not rerun
`init`. Restoration messages carry `state` and `mode` (`restore` or `autocomplete`). Forms
and the `states` spec share Gyral's single internals attachment.

---

# Effects and drivers

> Reducers return commands, side effects described as data. Drivers run them, with built-in concurrency, retries and cancellation, and answer with messages.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/

Reducers can't fetch, wait or write to storage, because they're pure. Instead they return
**commands**: plain objects that describe a side effect and say which message the outcome
becomes. A **driver** runs the command and answers with that message. Effects are data, and
they happen at the edges.

## Commands as data

```ts
// src/user.ts
import { define, html } from '@gyral/core';
import { get, type HttpError } from '@gyral/http';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const User = v.object({ name: v.string(), email: v.string() });

export type State =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Idle' }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Loading' }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Loaded'; readonly name: string; readonly email: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly reason: string };

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Load'; readonly id: number }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Loaded'; readonly name: string; readonly email: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly error: HttpError };

export const UserCard = define<State, Msg>()('my-user-card', {
  init: () => ({ _tag: 'Idle' }),
  intent: { Load: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Load', id: Number(value) }) },
  update: {
    Load: (_s, m) => [
      { _tag: 'Loading' },
      [
        get(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${String(m.id)}`, {
          schema: User,
          onSuccess: (user): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Loaded', ...user }),
          onFailure: (error): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }),
        }),
      ],
    ],
    Loaded: (_s, m) => ({ _tag: 'Loaded', name: m.name, email: m.email }),
    Failed: (_s, m) => ({ _tag: 'Failed', reason: m.error._tag }),
  },
  view: (s, i) => html`
    <button type="button" value="1" data-intent=${i.Load}>Load user 1</button>
    <p aria-live="polite">
      ${s._tag === 'Loaded' ? `${s.name} <${s.email}>` : s._tag === 'Failed' ? `Failed: ${s.reason}` : s._tag}
    </p>
  `,
});
```

`get(url, handlers)` builds a command for the `http` driver. The handlers are pure mappers:

- **`schema`** decodes the response with any Standard Schema, so `onSuccess` receives typed,
  validated data. A response that doesn't match becomes an `HttpDecodeError`.
- **`onSuccess`** turns the decoded body into a message.
- **`onFailure`** turns an error into a message. Errors are tagged data (`HttpStatusError`,
  `HttpNetworkError`, `HttpDecodeError`); nothing is ever thrown into the view. Leave it out and a
  failure goes to the [error channel](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/).

The request and its answer sit next to each other in one reducer, typed end to end, with no
"response category" strings to match up.

## Concurrency lanes

What should happen when the user types again before the last search returned? Gyral answers it
with a policy, not with stream operators. Each command runs in a **lane** (`key`, by default the
driver's name), and the lane has a policy:

| Policy    | In one lane                               | Use for                      |
| --------- | ----------------------------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| `merge`   | run every command concurrently (default)  | independent writes, logging  |
| `switch`  | cancel the one in flight, run the new one | search as you type, debounce |
| `exhaust` | ignore new commands while one runs        | submit buttons, refresh      |
| `queue`   | run one at a time, in order               | ordered saves                |

```ts
// src/search.ts
import type { Command } from '@gyral/core';
import { get } from '@gyral/http';

/** A newer query cancels the request in flight, so results never arrive out of order. */
export const search = <M>(query: string, toMsg: (body: unknown) => M): Command<M> =>
  get(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(query)}`, {
    key: 'search',
    concurrency: 'switch',
    onSuccess: toMsg,
  });
```

A cancelled command's `AbortSignal` aborts (so `fetch` stops), and its result is never
delivered. When a component is removed from the page, all its commands are cancelled the same
way, one microtask later; moving it cancels nothing.

## Built-in drivers

| Package         | Commands                                                                              |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@gyral/http`   | `get(url, handlers)`, `request(req, handlers)`, `submitForm(url, formData, handlers)` |
| `@gyral/time`   | `delay(ms, msg)`, `debounce(ms, msg)`, `every(ms, toMsg)`                             |
| `@gyral/router` | `navigate(url)`, `setHead(head)`, `listen(toMsg)`                                     |

More commands are handled by the component itself rather than a driver: an output (from
`outputs<Out>()`) goes to the [parent](https://gyral.dev/docs/components/#child-components-and-outputs),
`send(store, msg)` writes to a [store](https://gyral.dev/docs/stores/), `focus(selector)` moves
[focus](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#focus-is-a-command) after the next render, and `call(selector, method)`
[calls a method](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#calling-a-method-on-an-element) on an element after it.

### Commands that answer nothing

`focus()`, `call()`, an output, `navigate()` and `setHead()` return `Command<never>`: they
produce no message. `never` fits any message type, so they go in any reducer's command list, and in a
helper typed `Command<Msg>`, with no type argument:

```ts
// src/after-save.ts
import { focus, type Command } from '@gyral/core';
import { navigate } from '@gyral/router';

export type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'Saved' } | { readonly _tag: 'Failed' };

/** After a save: back to the list, with focus on its heading. */
export const afterSave = (): readonly Command<Msg>[] => [navigate('/items'), focus('h1')];
```

Your own are the same with no handlers at all: `command(log, text)` is a `Command<never>`. A
failure still reaches the [error channel](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/). With handlers, the message type
comes from what `onSuccess` and `onFailure` return, so explicit type arguments are rarely needed.

Debounce is a delay under `switch`: each keystroke's `debounce(300, msg)` cancels the pending
one. `delay` and `debounce` run on a delay-only driver, so an app that uses only them doesn't
bundle the code for `every`. Randomness is a command too, so models stay pure and tests can fix
the numbers: it's a six-line driver of your own (below).

## Writing a driver

A driver is a plain object with a `name` and a `run` function:

```ts
// src/clipboard.ts
import { command, defineDriver, type Command } from '@gyral/core';

/** Why a copy failed. */
export type CopyError = 'unavailable' | 'denied' | 'failed';

/** Writes text to the clipboard. */
export const clipboard = defineDriver<string, void, CopyError>({
  name: 'clipboard',
  run: (text) => navigator.clipboard.writeText(text),
  concurrency: 'switch',
  toError: (cause) =>
    cause instanceof TypeError
      ? 'unavailable'
      : cause instanceof DOMException && cause.name === 'NotAllowedError'
        ? 'denied'
        : 'failed',
});

export const copyText = <M>(text: string, copied: M, failed: (error: CopyError) => M): Command<M> =>
  command(clipboard, text, { onSuccess: () => copied, onFailure: failed });
```

- `run(input, { signal, emit })` returns the output or a promise of it. Abort work when `signal`
  aborts.
- `toError` turns whatever was thrown into the driver's typed error, which `onFailure` receives.
- `concurrency` is the default policy for the driver's commands; a command can override it.
- Retries aren't a driver option: wrap the driver where you choose it (next section).
- `defineDriver` only helps TypeScript infer the input, output and error types. Wrap the driver
  in typed command helpers like `copyText`, as the built-in packages do.

Nothing should run at import time: create resources when a command first runs, so modules are
safe to import on a server.

Randomness, for example:

```ts
// src/random.ts
import { command, defineDriver, type Command } from '@gyral/core';

const random = defineDriver<{ readonly min: number; readonly max: number }, number>({
  name: 'random',
  run: ({ min, max }) => min + Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)),
});

/** A whole number from `min` to `max`; tests substitute the `random` driver to fix it. */
export const randomInt = <M>(min: number, max: number, toMsg: (n: number) => M): Command<M> =>
  command(random, { min, max }, { onSuccess: toMsg });
```

### Drivers the app provides

A driver with no implementation of its own, such as a connection your app opens, a session or a
service only the entry point can build, is a **token**: `defineDriver<I, O, E>('session')`.
Commands built from it are fully typed, and it runs whatever an ancestor provides under that
name. If nothing does, the command fails with an error naming the driver and the component, so
there is no placeholder to write and no import order to get right:

```ts
// src/session.ts
import { command, defineDriver, type Command } from '@gyral/core';

export interface Move {
  readonly from: string;
  readonly to: string;
}

/** A token: the app's entry provides its implementation (below). */
export const session = defineDriver<Move, { readonly accepted: boolean }, string>('session');

export const sendMove = <M>(move: Move, answered: (accepted: boolean) => M): Command<M> =>
  command(session, move, { onSuccess: (r) => answered(r.accepted) });
```

The app's entry provides the implementation from the token itself. `session.provide(run)` is a
driver with the token's name, concurrency and `toError`, and a `run` checked against the token's
input and output, so a wrong type fails to compile and the name can't be mistyped. A token for a
stream is provided the same way, with `subscription(token, subscribe)`
([State Gyral doesn't own](https://gyral.dev/docs/outside-state/#a-store-per-page-provided-by-a-token)):

```ts
// src/app-drivers.ts
import { provideDrivers } from '@gyral/core';
import { session } from './session.js';

provideDrivers(document.body, [
  session.provide(async (move, { signal }) => {
    const body = JSON.stringify(move);
    const response = await fetch('/api/moves', { method: 'POST', body, signal });
    return { accepted: response.ok };
  }),
]);
```

### Retries

`retry(driver, { times, delayMs?, backoff?, jitter?, retryIf? })` from `@gyral/core` returns the
same driver, under the same name, with failures tried again after the delay (`'fixed'` or
`'exponential'`). `jitter: true` waits a random time between 0 and that delay, so many clients
don't retry in step. `retryIf(error)` decides which failures to retry; it receives the
driver's typed error (its `toError`, else the thrown value), and by default every failure is
retried. A cancellation (the command switched away, the component removed) ends it at once and
is never retried. Wrap the driver where you choose it, at app setup, in an element's `drivers`
or in a test, and apps that never retry don't bundle the code.

For `@gyral/http`, `makeHttpDriver({ timeoutMs })` gives each attempt a deadline: a slower
attempt fails with `HttpTimeoutError` (`url`, `timeoutMs`), and the retry starts a fresh one.
`retryableHttpError` retries only what a second try can fix: network errors, timeouts, 408, 429
and 5xx. It doesn't read `Retry-After`.

```ts
// src/main.ts
import { provideDrivers, retry } from '@gyral/core';
import { makeHttpDriver, retryableHttpError } from '@gyral/http';

provideDrivers(document.body, [
  retry(makeHttpDriver({ baseUrl: '/api', timeoutMs: 8_000 }), {
    times: 2,
    delayMs: 300,
    backoff: 'exponential',
    jitter: true,
    retryIf: retryableHttpError,
  }),
]);
```

`HttpError` is a union, so a `switch` that handles every case needs one for timeouts:

```ts
// src/errors.ts
import type { HttpError } from '@gyral/http';

export const describeError = (e: HttpError): string => {
  switch (e._tag) {
    case 'HttpStatusError':
      return `The server answered ${String(e.status)}.`;
    case 'HttpNetworkError':
      return 'You seem to be offline.';
    case 'HttpTimeoutError':
      return 'The server took too long to answer.';
    case 'HttpDecodeError':
      return 'The server sent something unexpected.';
  }
};
```

### Telling a refused request from no change

When a server (or a shared session) can refuse what the user asked for, don't infer the refusal
from a snapshot that didn't change: "same data" can mean refused, not yet processed, or a move
that changed nothing. Make the refusal a message of its own. A request with a reply maps the
refusal to its own variant through the command's `onFailure`; a feed that answers out of band
carries the request's id, so the component can tell its own refusal from someone else's update:

```ts
// src/moves.ts
import { command, defineDriver, type Command } from '@gyral/core';

interface Move {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly cell: number;
}
type Refusal = { readonly reason: string };

type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Accepted'; readonly id: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Refused'; readonly id: string; readonly reason: string };

/** The server answers 200 or a 409 with `{ reason }`; `toError` turns the 409 into a Refusal. */
const moves = defineDriver<Move, void, Refusal>({
  name: 'moves',
  run: async (move, { signal }) => {
    const res = await fetch('/api/moves', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(move), signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw (await res.json()) as Refusal;
  },
  toError: (cause) =>
    typeof cause === 'object' && cause !== null && 'reason' in cause
      ? { reason: String(cause.reason) }
      : { reason: 'unavailable' },
});

export const propose = (move: Move): Command<Msg> =>
  command(moves, move, {
    onSuccess: (): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Accepted', id: move.id }),
    onFailure: (refusal): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Refused', id: move.id, reason: refusal.reason }),
  });
```

The `Refused` reducer can then undo an optimistic change and show the reason. For form
submissions, `IntentRejected` is already this message ([Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/)).

### A copy button

With the driver above, a "Copy link" button is a message, a command and two answers:

```ts
// src/copy-link.ts
import { define, html, prop } from '@gyral/core';
import { copyText, type CopyError } from './clipboard.js';

export interface State {
  readonly status: 'idle' | 'copied' | CopyError;
}

export type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Copy' }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Copied' }
  | { readonly _tag: 'CopyFailed'; readonly error: CopyError };

const STATUS: Readonly<Record<State['status'], string>> = {
  idle: '',
  copied: 'Link copied.',
  unavailable: 'Copying needs a secure (https) page. Select the link and copy it instead.',
  denied: 'The browser blocked copying. Select the link and copy it instead.',
  failed: 'Copying failed. Select the link and copy it instead.',
};

export const CopyLink = define<State, Msg, { readonly url: string }>()('my-copy-link', {
  props: { url: prop.string({ required: true }) },
  init: () => ({ status: 'idle' }),
  intent: { Copy: () => ({ _tag: 'Copy' }) },
  update: {
    Copy: (s, _m, { props }) => [
      s,
      [copyText<Msg>(props.url, { _tag: 'Copied' }, (error) => ({ _tag: 'CopyFailed', error }))],
    ],
    Copied: () => ({ status: 'copied' }),
    CopyFailed: (_s, m) => ({ status: m.error }),
  },
  view: (s, i, { props }) => html`
    <label for="link">Link</label>
    <input id="link" readonly value=${props.url} />
    <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Copy}>Copy link</button>
    <p role="status">${STATUS[s.status]}</p>
  `,
});
```

- **`navigator.clipboard` exists only in a secure context**: https://, or localhost. Elsewhere
  reading `writeText` throws a `TypeError`, which `toError` turns into `unavailable`.
- **Browsers write only during a user activation.** Return the command from the reducer of the
  click's message, as above: with a synchronous parser, it starts while the click is still
  being handled. Started later, the browser rejects it with `NotAllowedError`, `denied` here.
- **Tests never touch the real clipboard**: they substitute the driver by name,
  `el.drivers = [fakeDriver(clipboard)]`, a fake that takes the driver's name
  ([Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/#fake-drivers-and-commands)).

## Streaming results with emit

A driver can deliver more than one result: `emit(output)` sends a value through the command's
`onSuccess` while the command keeps running. Routers, timers, sockets and observers work this
way. A streaming `run` usually returns a promise that never resolves, and stops when `signal`
aborts:

```ts
// src/online.ts
import { command, defineDriver, type Command } from '@gyral/core';

/** Streams `navigator.onLine` now and on every change, until the component disconnects. */
export const online = defineDriver<void, boolean>({
  name: 'online',
  run: (_input, { signal, emit }) =>
    new Promise<boolean>(() => {
      const report = (): void => {
        emit(navigator.onLine);
      };
      report();
      window.addEventListener('online', report, { signal });
      window.addEventListener('offline', report, { signal });
    }),
});

export const watchOnline = <M>(toMsg: (online: boolean) => M): Command<M> =>
  command(online, undefined, { onSuccess: toMsg, concurrency: 'switch' });
```

List a stream in the component's [`subscriptions`](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/#subscriptions), and it runs
while the component is on the page. For a source Gyral doesn't own, such as signals, a Redux-style store or a socket, `subscription()` from `@gyral/core` writes
this plumbing for you: see [State Gyral doesn't own](https://gyral.dev/docs/outside-state/).

## Substituting drivers

Commands carry their driver, so most apps need no wiring. To substitute one, for a test fake
or a configured instance, Gyral looks drivers up **by name**, in this order:

1. the element's own `el.drivers`;
2. the nearest driver provider above it: a `<gyral-drivers>` element or
   `provideDrivers(element, drivers)`;
3. the driver object on the command.

Supply drivers as a list: each one goes under its own name, so there is no key to mistype. For
example, give every request on the page default headers, once, at the app's entry:

```ts
// src/entry-client.ts
import { provideDrivers } from '@gyral/core';
import { csrfFromMeta, makeHttpDriver } from '@gyral/http';

provideDrivers(document.body, [makeHttpDriver({ headers: csrfFromMeta('csrf-token') })]);
```

A record keyed by name, `{ http: makeHttpDriver(…) }`, works in the same places and reads well
for fakes in tests. Its keys must be the drivers' names, because a command looks its driver up
by the driver's own name: development warns when a key isn't the name of the driver under it
([G0045](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0045)), and throws for two drivers of one name in a list
([G0044](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0044)).

A component starts its `init` commands after its first render, a microtask after it connects.
So `provideDrivers` anywhere in the entry's synchronous code is in time, even when the entry
imports its components first and their elements are already in the page. After an `await` it
is too late for those elements: provide drivers before awaiting, or create the element in code
and set its `drivers` before inserting it. A token nothing provides is reported as
[G0043](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0043).

`csrfFromMeta` reads `<meta name="csrf-token">` when each request runs, so components never read
the DOM for it. The driver's headers are the one place a CSRF token from a `<meta>` is
configured. Development builds warn once when a
`POST`, `PUT`, `PATCH` or `DELETE` goes out without the token while the page has a CSRF
`<meta>`. [Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/) uses the same lookup to swap in fakes.

## On the server

Commands never run during a server render: there is no interpreter, no timer and no network.
Do async work in the route handler and pass results as props. After hydration, the browser
starts `init`'s commands and the component's subscriptions, so `listen()` begins exactly where
the server left off. See [Server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/).

---

# Error handling

> How Gyral reports each failure once, lets a parent catch a child's failure, shows a component's fallback and keeps a server-rendered page going.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/

Code fails: a reducer reads a field that isn't there, a view meets data it didn't expect, a
driver's server is down. Gyral catches every failure in a component, wraps it in a
`GyralError` and sends it through **one channel**, so nothing escapes into the page as an
uncaught exception and nothing is only logged.

Expected failures are different: a request that can fail should say what its failure becomes.
Give its command an `onFailure` that maps the error to a message, and handle that message in
`update` like any other ([Effects and drivers](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/)). The channel on this page is for
the failures you didn't plan for.

## One channel

A `GyralError` carries `component` (the host's tag), `phase` (where it failed), `msg` (the
message tag, intent name or driver) and `cause` (what was thrown). In order:

1. **Devtools** shows an `error` row in the timeline (development).
2. **A parent can catch it.** A bubbling, composed, cancelable `ErrorEvent('error')` is
   dispatched on the failing component. An ancestor that listens for it is a **boundary**; it
   claims the failure with `preventDefault()`.
3. **The component's own fallback runs.** Its `error(failure, state)` view renders when `init`
   or the view threw; its optional `Errored` reducer receives failed updates, parsers and
   commands.
4. **Unless a parent claimed it, it is reported** with
   [`reportError()`](https://developer.mozilla.org/docs/Web/API/reportError): `window`'s `error`
   event and your monitoring see it, once.

| Phase       | What threw                                                                 | What happens                                                                |
| ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `init`      | `init`                                                                     | No state: `error(failure, undefined)` renders, or the component stays empty |
| `update`    | a reducer                                                                  | Nothing changes: the state is kept and its commands don't run; `Errored`    |
| `view`      | the view                                                                   | `error(failure, state)` renders, or the previous DOM stays                  |
| `parse`     | an intent parser (throws or rejects)                                       | No message; `Errored`                                                       |
| `command`   | an `onSuccess`/`onFailure` mapper, or a driver failure without `onFailure` | No message; `Errored`                                                       |
| `hook`      | an element hook                                                            | Reported; the other hooks of that render still run                          |
| `store`     | a store reducer or a subscriber                                            | The store is unchanged / the other subscribers are still notified           |
| `subscribe` | a subscription's unsubscribe                                               | Reported; the command still stops                                           |

`el.send()` never throws to its caller, and a failure inside `error` or `Errored` is reported
once, never looped. `Errored` is a framework message name, like `PropsChanged`.

## A component's own fallback

`error(failure, state)` renders instead of the view when `init` (then `state` is `undefined`)
or the view throws. `Errored` lets the component switch to an error state, or reset:

```ts
// src/order-list.ts
import { command, define, defineDriver, html, type GyralError } from '@gyral/core';

interface Order {
  readonly id: string;
  readonly total: number;
}
type State =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Ready'; readonly orders: readonly Order[] }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Broken'; readonly reason: string };
type Msg =
  { readonly _tag: 'Refresh' } | { readonly _tag: 'Loaded'; readonly orders: readonly Order[] };

const orders = defineDriver<undefined, readonly Order[]>({
  name: 'orders',
  run: async (_input, { signal }) => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/orders', { signal });
    return (await response.json()) as readonly Order[];
  },
});
const refresh = () =>
  command(orders, undefined, { onSuccess: (list): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Loaded', orders: list }) });

export const OrderList = define<State, Msg>()('order-list', {
  init: () => [{ _tag: 'Ready', orders: [] }, [refresh()]],
  intent: { Refresh: () => ({ _tag: 'Refresh' }) },
  update: {
    Refresh: (s) => [s, [refresh()]],
    Loaded: (_s, m) => ({ _tag: 'Ready', orders: m.orders }),
    // Any failed update, parse or command of this component. The driver failing lands here
    // too, because this command has no onFailure.
    Errored: (_s, m) => ({ _tag: 'Broken', reason: m.error.phase }),
  },
  view: (s, i) =>
    s._tag === 'Broken'
      ? html`<p role="alert">Orders are unavailable (${s.reason}).</p>
          <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Refresh}>Try again</button>`
      : html`<ul>
          ${s.orders.map((o) => html`<li>${o.id}: ${o.total}</li>`)}
        </ul>`,
  error: (failure: GyralError) =>
    html`<p role="alert">Orders failed to show (${failure.phase}).</p>`,
});
```

## A parent boundary

A parent catches a child's failure with the intents it already has: listen for `error` on the
child, read the `GyralError` from the event, and call `preventDefault()` to claim it. A claimed
failure isn't reported, so report it yourself if you still want it in your telemetry. To retry,
re-mount the child (render it in a different template, or give it a new key in `each()`): its
`init` runs again.

```ts
// src/dashboard.ts
import { define, html, type GyralError } from '@gyral/core';

interface State {
  readonly attempt: number;
  readonly failed: boolean;
}
type Msg = { readonly _tag: 'WidgetFailed' } | { readonly _tag: 'Retry' };

export const Dashboard = define<State, Msg>()('my-dashboard', {
  init: () => ({ attempt: 0, failed: false }),
  intent: {
    WidgetFailed: ({ event }) => {
      const failure = (event as ErrorEvent).error as GyralError;
      event.preventDefault(); // claimed: this boundary handles it, the page doesn't
      console.info('the chart failed in', failure.phase);
      return { _tag: 'WidgetFailed' };
    },
    Retry: () => ({ _tag: 'Retry' }),
  },
  update: {
    WidgetFailed: (s) => ({ ...s, failed: true }),
    Retry: (s) => ({ attempt: s.attempt + 1, failed: false }),
  },
  view: (s, i) =>
    s.failed
      ? html`<p role="alert">The chart is unavailable.</p>
          <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Retry}>Retry</button>`
      : s.attempt % 2 === 0
        ? html`<div>
            <sales-chart data-intent=${i.WidgetFailed} data-intent-on="error"></sales-chart>
          </div>`
        : html`<p>
            <sales-chart data-intent=${i.WidgetFailed} data-intent-on="error"></sales-chart>
          </p>`,
});
```

The event stops at the document, so `window` hears an unclaimed failure only once, through
`reportError`.

## Monitoring

Every unclaimed failure reaches `window` once. Listen there; `event.error` is the `GyralError`:

```ts
// src/telemetry.ts
import { GyralError } from '@gyral/core';

window.addEventListener('error', (event) => {
  if (!(event.error instanceof GyralError)) return;
  const { component, phase, msg, cause } = event.error;
  navigator.sendBeacon(
    '/telemetry',
    JSON.stringify({ component, phase, msg, cause: String(cause) }),
  );
});
```

Production builds report the same errors with short messages; the codes are explained on the
[error codes](https://gyral.dev/errors/) page. For your own tooling, the same table (code, group, message,
arguments, link) ships with the package as `@gyral/core/errors.json`:

```ts
import table from '@gyral/core/errors.json' with { type: 'json' };
```

## On the server

A component whose `init` or view throws during [server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/)
renders its `error` view (or nothing), marked `data-gyral-error` and without a seed. The rest of
the page renders, and the browser starts that component fresh. `renderPage`'s `onError` hears
each failure (default `console.error`). With `onError: 'throw'`, `renderPage` renders the page
to a string first and throws before any byte is sent, so the route can answer with its error
page:

```ts
// src/server/orders-page.ts
import { html, type GyralError } from '@gyral/core';
import { renderPage } from '@gyral/ssr';

declare const report: (error: GyralError) => void;
const body = html`<order-list></order-list>`;

// One failing component shouldn't take the page down: it shows its fallback.
export const ordersPage = (): Response =>
  renderPage({ title: 'Orders', body, onError: (error) => report(error) });

// This page is all or nothing: answer 500 with an error page instead.
export function checkoutPage(): Response {
  try {
    return renderPage({ title: 'Checkout', body, onError: 'throw' });
  } catch {
    return new Response('Something went wrong', { status: 500 });
  }
}
```

Data loading happens before `renderPage`, so the route handler already owns the error page for
its own failures.

## In tests

`reportError` counts as an uncaught error, and Vitest fails a test run on one. That's what you
want for failures you didn't plan. When a test makes a component fail on purpose, collect the
failures with `collectErrors()` from `@gyral/testing` and assert on them:

```ts
// src/order-list.browser.test.ts
import { settled } from '@gyral/core';
import { collectErrors, fakeDriver } from '@gyral/testing';
import { afterEach, expect, it } from 'vitest';
import { OrderList } from './order-list.js';

let collected: ReturnType<typeof collectErrors> | undefined;
afterEach(() => collected?.stop());

it('shows the error state when the orders fail to load', async () => {
  collected = collectErrors();
  const el = new OrderList();
  el.drivers = [
    fakeDriver('orders', () => {
      throw new Error('down');
    }),
  ];
  document.body.append(el);
  await settled();
  expect(collected.errors.map((e) => e.phase)).toEqual(['command']);
  expect(el.shadowRoot?.textContent).toContain('unavailable');
});
```

In a model test, `step()` accepts `Errored`, so you can test that reducer without a DOM.

## Debugging a failure

Start with the production diagnostic code, for example `Gyral G0010`. The
[diagnostics reference](https://gyral.dev/errors/) expands it into the cause and a suggested fix. A development
build includes the explanation; the [devtools panel](https://gyral.dev/docs/devtools/) shows the message,
previous/next state, component and command lane around the failure. Inspect the underlying
`GyralError.cause` without putting private user data into shared logs.

Distinguish three outcomes:

- A parser returning `undefined` ignores an event; no message reaches the reducer.
- A schema failure in `form()` or `field()` produces `IntentRejected`, which belongs in your
  validation UI. It is expected invalid input, not a thrown defect.
- A parser, reducer, view, hook or command mapper throwing uses the error channel described
  above. A planned driver failure with `onFailure` instead becomes its typed message.

On the server, `onError(error)` observes component failures. Without a throwing policy, a
failed component can render its fallback while the page continues. `onError: 'throw'` makes
the render fail before returning the response; chunked output cannot change an HTTP status
after bytes have been sent. See [Server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/).

For a hydration mismatch, reproduce with the production build and the exact server/client
assets. Check stale HTML, unseeded current time, locale differences, invalid parser-repaired
markup, and third-party changes before scripts arrive. Use `mountSsr()` and `hydrated()` to
exercise real server markup; they report mounting/hydration problems. Keep a small failing
test before changing the implementation. See [Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/),
[Security](https://gyral.dev/docs/security/) and [Versioning](https://gyral.dev/docs/versioning/).

---

# Browser storage

> Typed localStorage and IndexedDB drivers: persist values, watch settings, query records and run atomic transactions.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/browser-storage/

Storage is a driver effect. Keep reads/writes out of reducers, init and views. The optional
`@gyral/core/storage` entry adds no storage code to apps that do not import it. Factories and
imports are safe on the server; browser access starts only when commands run.

## localStorage

```ts
// src/theme-storage.ts
import { command, define, html } from '@gyral/core';
import { makeLocalStorageDriver, type StorageError, type StorageOutput } from '@gyral/core/storage';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const settings = makeLocalStorageDriver(v.object({ theme: v.string() }), { prefix: 'app:' });
interface State {
  readonly theme: string;
  readonly error?: StorageError;
}
type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Stored'; readonly result: StorageOutput<{ theme: string }> }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly error: StorageError }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Dark' };

export const Theme = define<State, Msg>()('my-storage-theme', {
  init: () => ({ theme: 'light' }),
  subscriptions: () => [
    command(
      settings,
      { _tag: 'Watch', key: 'settings' },
      {
        key: 'settings-watch',
        onSuccess: (result) => ({ _tag: 'Stored', result }),
        onFailure: (error) => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }),
      },
    ),
  ],
  intent: { Dark: true },
  update: {
    Stored: (s, m) =>
      m.result._tag === 'StorageChanged' && m.result.entry.found
        ? { theme: m.result.entry.value.theme }
        : s,
    Failed: (s, m) => ({ ...s, error: m.error }),
    Dark: (s) => [
      s,
      [
        command(
          settings,
          {
            _tag: 'Write',
            key: 'settings',
            value: { theme: 'dark' },
          },
          { key: 'settings-write', onFailure: (error) => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }) },
        ),
      ],
    ],
  },
  view: (s, i) =>
    html`<p>${s.theme}</p>
      <button type="button" data-intent=${i.Dark}>Dark theme</button>`,
});
```

`Read { key }` returns `StorageValue` with `entry: { found: false }` or
`{ found: true, value }`. `Write { key, value }`, `Remove { key }` and `Clear` return
completion tags. Clear removes only the configured prefix (default empty: all localStorage).
Watch emits an initial snapshot, then changes from driver writes (`source: 'driver'`) and
native events in other tabs (`'tab'`). Direct same-tab localStorage writes are not observed.
Removal/clear emit absence. A malformed Watch value emits `StorageDecodeFailed` and leaves
the watch running; Read rejects with `StorageDecodeError`. Access/quota/security failures
go through `StorageAccessError` and command `onFailure`. Handle both watch output variants.

The Standard Schema decodes parsed JSON, including async validation. If it transforms the
input, configure `encode(value)` to reconstruct its JSON input shape. No transactions or
cross-tab atomicity are promised. Use distinct command keys for watches and writes. Abort
removes listeners and suppresses late decoder results. Tests put `fakeDriver(settings)`, which
takes the driver's name, in `el.drivers = [fake]`, or use an isolated
`storage: () => storageObject`.

Initial watches belong in `subscriptions`: the server's seed hydrates first, then browser
storage updates the model. Keep server-rendered state JSON-compatible.

## IndexedDB

Use the separate `@gyral/core/indexeddb` entry for structured records, object stores,
indexes, migrations and atomic transaction batches. It uses the same command and fake-driver
conventions, with native IndexedDB semantics:

```ts
// src/contacts-storage.ts
import { command, type Command } from '@gyral/core';
import {
  makeIndexedDBDriver,
  type IndexedDBError,
  type IndexedDBOutput,
} from '@gyral/core/indexeddb';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const stores = { contacts: v.object({ id: v.string(), name: v.string() }) };
type Contact = v.InferOutput<typeof stores.contacts>;
const contacts = makeIndexedDBDriver(stores, {
  database: 'address-book',
  version: 1,
  upgrade: (db, oldVersion) => {
    if (oldVersion < 1) {
      const store = db.createObjectStore('contacts', { keyPath: 'id' });
      store.createIndex('name', 'name');
    }
  },
});
type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Database'; readonly result: IndexedDBOutput<typeof stores> }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly error: IndexedDBError };
const handlers = {
  onSuccess: (result: IndexedDBOutput<typeof stores>): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Database', result }),
  onFailure: (error: IndexedDBError): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }),
};
export const readContact = (id: string): Command<Msg> =>
  command(contacts, { _tag: 'Read', store: 'contacts', key: id }, handlers);
export const saveContacts = (values: readonly Contact[]): Command<Msg> =>
  command(
    contacts,
    {
      _tag: 'Transaction',
      operations: values.map(
        (value) =>
          ({
            _tag: 'Put',
            store: 'contacts',
            value,
          }) as const,
      ),
    },
    { ...handlers, concurrency: 'queue' },
  );
export const findContacts = (name: string): Command<Msg> =>
  command(
    contacts,
    {
      _tag: 'Query',
      store: 'contacts',
      index: 'name',
      range: { _tag: 'Only', key: name },
      limit: 20,
    },
    handlers,
  );
```

`Read` returns `Record` with a found/absent entry. `Put` returns its actual primary key
(optional input key, or the store's inline/auto-increment key); `Delete` returns `Deleted`.
`Query` returns `Records` with primary keys and decoded values. Queries require a positive
integer limit, allow `direction` (`next`, `prev`, `nextunique`, `prevunique`), and optional
range data: Only/Lower/Upper with `key`, or Bound with `lower`/`upper`. Bounds accept `open`,
`lowerOpen` and `upperOpen` as appropriate. Store names/record values are typed; index names
are strings defined by the application migration and checked by the browser.

A nonempty Transaction batch queues all requests synchronously across its stores and
returns `Committed { results }` in operation order after the native transaction completes.
Read-only batches use readonly transactions; batches containing Put/Delete use readwrite.
A failure aborts the whole batch. Stored Read/Query values decode after commit, including
async schemas; a decode failure carries `committed: true`, so earlier batch writes remain.
An optional `encode(store, value)` reconstructs a transforming schema's stored input shape.

The version and synchronous `upgrade(db, oldVersion, newVersion, transaction)` callback
belong to the application. Queue migration requests before returning; never await. A blocked
upgrade rejects with `IndexedDBBlockedError`, aborts any abandoned late upgrade and closes
any late connection. Retry explicitly once older connections close. Migration/access/native
transaction failures use `IndexedDBAccessError`; invalid query limits/empty batches use
`IndexedDBInputError`; invalid persisted records use `IndexedDBDecodeError`.

Abort attempts rollback and suppresses late output; it cannot undo an already committed
transaction. Connections close after each native transaction, before async decoding, and
on versionchange. No resources open on import/factory creation. Start browser reads after
the first render (init commands or subscriptions), and keep SSR model state JSON-compatible.
Tests substitute `fakeDriver(contacts)` by name (`indexeddb` by default). No storage watches
or automatic cross-tab synchronization are promised for this driver.

---

# Network streams

> Native EventSource and WebSocket drivers: receive validated streams, send messages and handle connection lifecycles.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/network-streams/

Optional `@gyral/http/sse` and `@gyral/http/websocket` entries use browser-native transports.
They are separate from the fetch entry, add no runtime dependencies, and open no resources
on import or factory creation. Use normal commands, declarative subscriptions and fake
substitution by driver name. Feeds start after the first render, preserving SSR seeds.

## Server-sent events

```ts
// src/server-count.ts
import { command, define, html } from '@gyral/core';
import {
  makeEventSourceDriver,
  type EventSourceError,
  type EventSourceOutput,
} from '@gyral/http/sse';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const schema = v.object({ count: v.number() });
const feed = makeEventSourceDriver(schema, { events: ['count'], withCredentials: false });
type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Feed'; readonly value: EventSourceOutput<v.InferOutput<typeof schema>> }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly error: EventSourceError };
interface State {
  readonly count: number;
  readonly status: string;
}
export const Counter = define<State, Msg>()('my-server-count', {
  init: () => ({ count: 0, status: 'connecting' }),
  subscriptions: () => [
    command(
      feed,
      { url: '/events' },
      {
        onSuccess: (value) => ({ _tag: 'Feed', value }),
        onFailure: (error) => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }),
      },
    ),
  ],
  update: {
    Feed: (s, m) => {
      switch (m.value._tag) {
        case 'EventSourceMessage':
          return { ...s, count: m.value.data.count };
        case 'EventSourceState':
          return { ...s, status: m.value.state };
        case 'EventSourceDecodeFailed':
          return { ...s, status: 'invalid event' };
      }
    },
    Failed: (s) => ({ ...s, status: 'closed' }),
  },
  view: (s) =>
    html`<output>${s.count}</output>
      <p role="status">${s.status}</p>`,
});
```

The driver always observes `message` and adds configured named events (no wildcard native
listener). `EventSourceMessage` preserves `eventType` and `lastEventId`; empty IDs are valid.
Default parsing is JSON followed by Standard Schema validation. Use `parse(text)` for another
text format. Async decoders preserve arrival order. Bad JSON/schema data emits
`EventSourceDecodeFailed { issues, eventType, lastEventId }` without ending the connection.

Native EventSource owns GET requests, cookie credentials, reconnection, server `retry:`
timing and Last-Event-ID. `withCredentials` configures cross-origin credentials; same-origin
cookies follow native behavior. CONNECTING errors report connecting state and keep the same
source. Terminal CLOSED errors report closed state and reject with `EventSourceError` through
`onFailure`; detailed HTTP status/body are unavailable. The driver adds no second retry loop.
Abort removes listeners, closes the source and suppresses pending decoded results.

Headers, POST streams and fetch-based transports are outside this driver. Event IDs do not
guarantee exactly-once delivery or replay; handle deduplication/resynchronization in your
protocol. Tests put `fakeDriver(feed)`, which takes the driver's name (`sse`, or the configured
one), in `el.drivers = [fake]` and call `fake.emitNext(...)` to deliver events/states.

## WebSocket

```ts
// src/native-chat.ts
import { command, define, html, retry } from '@gyral/core';
import {
  makeWebSocketDriver,
  type WebSocketError,
  type WebSocketOutput,
} from '@gyral/http/websocket';
import * as v from 'valibot';

const schema = v.object({ text: v.string() });
const raw = makeWebSocketDriver(schema, {
  encode: (value: { text: string }) => JSON.stringify(value),
});
const socket = retry(raw, {
  times: 3,
  delayMs: 500,
  backoff: 'exponential',
  jitter: true,
  retryIf: (error) => error._tag === 'WebSocketClosedError' && error.code === 1006,
});
interface State {
  readonly live: boolean;
  readonly text: string;
  readonly status: string;
}
type Msg =
  | { readonly _tag: 'Socket'; readonly value: WebSocketOutput<v.InferOutput<typeof schema>> }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Failed'; readonly error: WebSocketError }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Send'; readonly text: string }
  | { readonly _tag: 'Stop' };
const handlers = {
  onSuccess: (value: WebSocketOutput<v.InferOutput<typeof schema>>): Msg => ({
    _tag: 'Socket',
    value,
  }),
  onFailure: (error: WebSocketError): Msg => ({ _tag: 'Failed', error }),
};
export const Chat = define<State, Msg>()('my-native-chat', {
  init: () => ({ live: true, text: '', status: 'connecting' }),
  subscriptions: (s) =>
    s.live
      ? [
          command(
            socket,
            {
              _tag: 'Connect',
              connection: 'room',
              url: 'wss://example.test/chat',
            },
            { ...handlers, key: 'room-connect' },
          ),
        ]
      : [],
  intent: { Send: ({ value }) => ({ _tag: 'Send', text: value ?? '' }), Stop: true },
  update: {
    Send: (s, m) => [
      s,
      [
        command(
          socket,
          {
            _tag: 'Send',
            connection: 'room',
            value: { text: m.text },
          },
          { ...handlers, key: 'room-send' },
        ),
      ],
    ],
    Stop: (s) => [
      s,
      [
        command(
          socket,
          {
            _tag: 'Close',
            connection: 'room',
            code: 1000,
          },
          { ...handlers, key: 'room-close' },
        ),
      ],
    ],
    Failed: (s, m) => ({ ...s, live: false, status: m.error._tag }),
    Socket: (s, m) => {
      switch (m.value._tag) {
        case 'WebSocketMessage':
          return { ...s, text: m.value.data.text };
        case 'WebSocketState':
          return { ...s, status: m.value.state };
        case 'WebSocketDecodeFailed':
          return { ...s, status: 'invalid message' };
        case 'WebSocketClosed':
          return m.value.requested || (m.value.code === 1000 && m.value.wasClean)
            ? { ...s, live: false, status: 'closed' }
            : { ...s, status: 'reconnecting' };
        case 'WebSocketSent':
          return s; // enqueued, awaiting application acknowledgement
        case 'WebSocketCloseRequested':
          return s;
      }
    },
  },
```
