Use `output` for a computed result and a restrained status/live region for asynchronous
results that need announcing. Give a busy region `aria-busy` when appropriate. Do not announce
the whole page on every render. Use `dialog.showModal()` through the [`?modal` binding](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#dialogs-and-popovers) for modal
interaction, and keep a visible close control and a useful accessible name.

Set the document's `lang` and text direction. Keep machine date values locale-neutral and
isolate unknown-direction names with `bdi`. Honor `prefers-reduced-motion`; Gyral skips its
view transition when reduced motion is requested, but your own CSS animations need the same
care. Color must not be the only signal of selection, errors or status.

## Verify the real interface

Use browser tests to check roles, names, keyboard actions, focus after errors, Escape/close
behavior and focus return. Run axe on the rendered document and its shadow roots; the Gyral
repository's `pnpm ui:check` runs axe, overflow and console checks across desktop/phone and
light/dark. Apps own their equivalent checks. Automated checks catch some defects; also
exercise keyboard-only and screen-reader flows for your important tasks.

See [Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/) for browser helpers and [Browser support](https://gyral.dev/docs/browser-support/)
for enhancement behavior.

---

# Performance

> Measure Gyral's production payload, rendering work and hydration cost, then use keyed rows, structural sharing and islands where they help.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/performance/

Measure your production page before changing its update strategy. Include the entry, static
imports and modules the page actually fetches; a small entry can still load a large set of
component, hydration and fallback chunks.

## Rendering and keyed rows

Reducers run immediately. One scheduler batches DOM work in a microtask, renders parents
before children, and runs focus and other post-render work after the commit. A component
renders only when its state, a declared prop or a declared store's value has changed since its
last render, so a message whose reducer returns the same state costs no render: return `s`
itself when nothing changes, not a copy. When a view does render, unchanged binding values do
not rewrite the DOM. Keep views pure and deterministic: a view that reads anything else shows
stale values, and development warns about it ([G0017](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0017)).

Use `each(items, key, row, pick?)` for lists that insert, remove or reorder items. It skips a
row when its item reference and picked inputs are unchanged. Preserve unchanged objects in
your reducers and put changing external row inputs in `pick`; do not capture outer view state
in the row function. A `pick` that returns a new nested value every render defeats the check;
make its references stable, or compare with `each(items, key, row, { pick, equals })`.
Development checks and the row-purity lint help detect mistakes. See
[Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#lists) and [Update](https://gyral.dev/docs/update/).

Child components receive props by property. Unchanged declared props avoid a prop-triggered
render; a child's own messages and stores can still update it. Mutating an object in place
can hide a real change, while rebuilding every unchanged object defeats structural sharing.
For a costly subtree, first isolate it as a component with explicit inputs and measure again.

## Production compilation and payload

Use `gyral()` for production builds. It compiles template strings and binding paths
ahead of time and removes development diagnostics. A client-only app can use
`clientOnly: true` to exclude hydration machinery when no server markup needs it. This is a
build contract: do not use that option for a server-rendered page.

The repository's `pnpm size --json` measures production JavaScript with gzip level 9 and
reports the initial payload separately from all chunks. `pnpm size:check` enforces example
budgets. The [package overview](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#whats-inside) gives measurements of Gyral's
examples; they are examples, not a guarantee of your app's size. Compare versions with the same build options and assets.

## Hydration and loading

Hydration adopts server nodes rather than rebuilding the page. Its first view must agree with
the server's state, props, stores and formatted text. Recovery from a mismatch adds work and
can disturb user input. Read [Server rendering](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/) and use production
hydration tests, including forms edited before scripts arrive.

Choose islands when a region can wait until visible, idle or interaction. Keep initial HTML
useful and ensure keyboard users can reach the interactive part. Preload the modules a page
needs using its build manifest; avoid preloading every route just to make one navigation
faster. Automatic component loading and manual route splitting should be measured on the
whole page, including their loader and preload overhead. See
[Code splitting](https://gyral.dev/docs/code-splitting/) and [Rendering modes](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/).

## Reproduce a speed claim

The [Gyral benchmarks](https://github.com/gyraljs/benchmarks) build the same six
client-rendered apps with Gyral from npm and with current React, Preact, Vue, Svelte, Solid and
Lit. Each run's [raw data and notes](https://github.com/gyraljs/benchmarks/tree/main/results)
describe the machine, versions and variation, so compare frameworks within one run only. They
measure small apps in one browser, not server rendering or your application.

For your page, record network payloads and a browser performance trace for the action users
care about. Separate script, layout, paint and frame wait; fewer reducer milliseconds need
not make the visible action faster. Warm up, repeat the same tasks, retain raw results and
compare in one environment. Check input correctness alongside timings. For bursty external
sources, evaluate `renderOnFrame`, or a subscription's `coalesce: 'frame'` and `equals`
([State Gyral doesn't own](https://gyral.dev/docs/outside-state/#subscription)); discrete clicks and submits
usually need the default microtask rendering. See [Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/).

---

# Packages

> Every @gyral package, what it's for, how to install it, and the optional build tools Gyral works with.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/

Gyral is a set of small packages under the `@gyral` scope on npm, plus `create-gyral`, which
sets up a new app. Every app needs `@gyral/core`; add the others when you need them. All ten
packages are released together with the same version number (0.3.8), are ES modules with
TypeScript types, and are published from GitHub Actions with
[npm provenance](https://docs.npmjs.com/generating-provenance-statements).

## Core

| Package       | What it gives you                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@gyral/core` | `define()`, intents and `on()`, update and commands, subscriptions, stores, forms, `subscription()`, and the view layer: `html`, `svg`, `css`, `each`, `keyed`, `raw`, hooks. `/vite` has `gyral()`, the Vite plugins (template compiler, component loading, element typings), `/eslint` the lint rules. |

```sh
npm install @gyral/core
```

`@gyral/core/storage` and `@gyral/core/indexeddb` are optional entry points in the same
package. They provide separate native [localStorage and IndexedDB drivers](https://gyral.dev/docs/browser-storage/).
Apps that do not import them carry no storage driver code.

## Optional packages

| Package           | What it gives you                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@gyral/http`     | The `http` driver: `get`, `request`, `submitForm`, typed errors, schema decoding. `@gyral/http/testing` has `fakeHttp`.                                                                                                                                                                |
| `@gyral/router`   | Typed route tables, `listen`, `navigate`, `setHead`, browser and memory history.                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| `@gyral/time`     | `delay`, `debounce` and `every` as commands; an app that only delays doesn't bundle `every`.                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `@gyral/ssr`      | Server rendering: `renderPage`, `renderToString`, `contentSecurityPolicy`, `styleHashes`, `formAction`. `@gyral/ssr/static` prerenders and serves builds and writes component style hashes, `@gyral/ssr/node` mounts a fetch handler on Node's `http` and runs the development server. |
| `@gyral/testing`  | `step`, `run`, `viewOf`, `subscriptionsFor`, `outputsIn`, `mount`, `parse`, fake drivers, virtual time, `mountSsr` and `hydrated`. `@gyral/testing/vitest` renders server markup for browser tests.                                                                                    |
| `@gyral/devtools` | The in-page devtools panel, for development builds.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `@gyral/mcp`      | An MCP server for coding agents: it searches these docs, looks up exact API signatures, reads the examples, scaffolds components and typechecks snippets against your project. Hosted at `https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp`.                                                                  |
| `@gyral/codemod`  | Rewrites an app's source for a release's API changes, `npx @gyral/codemod 0.3.8`, and lists what it leaves for you. Run it with `npx`; there is nothing to install.                                                                                                                    |

```sh
npm install @gyral/http @gyral/router @gyral/time
npm install @gyral/ssr
npm install -D @gyral/testing @gyral/devtools
```

The same `@gyral/http` installation includes optional `@gyral/http/sse` and
`@gyral/http/websocket` entries for [native network streams](https://gyral.dev/docs/network-streams/).
The fetch entry does not include those transports.

`@gyral/mcp` is a stdio server your agent starts with `npx -y @gyral/mcp`, from your project
directory. It answers from the docs, API and examples of its own version, bundled at build time,
so it works offline. `gyral-mcp http` runs a read-only Streamable HTTP server instead; Gyral hosts one at
`https://mcp.gyral.dev/mcp`, with no token. Setup for Claude Code,
VS Code, Cursor, Codex and other clients is in
[Use Gyral with coding agents](https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/).

## create-gyral

`npm create gyral@latest` asks for a directory and a template, `basic` (client-rendered) or
`ssr` (server-rendered and hydrated), and writes an app that depends on the matching `@gyral/*`
release. [Getting started](https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/#create-a-project) walks through it.

## Optional peer dependencies

No Gyral package asks you to install another library at runtime. The build tools Gyral plugs
into are optional peer dependencies: install the ones you use.

| Package          | Optional peers                                                                            |
| ---------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `@gyral/core`    | `vite` ^8 (preset and compiler), `eslint` 9 or 10 (the plugin), `parse5` (compiler check) |
| `@gyral/ssr`     | `vite` ^8 (the development server in `@gyral/ssr/node`)                                   |
| `@gyral/testing` | `vitest` ^4.1 or ^5 (only for `@gyral/testing/vitest`)                                    |
| `@gyral/mcp`     | `typescript` 5 or 6 (for `check_snippet`, which uses your project's compiler)             |

Validation in `@gyral/core`, `@gyral/http` and `@gyral/ssr` accepts any
[Standard Schema](https://standardschema.dev) library; Gyral depends only on its types.

Any custom element works next to Gyral components, including ones built with Lit; install that
library yourself if you use it. Upgrading an existing app? See
[Versioning and stability](https://gyral.dev/docs/versioning/).

### One version of every package

`@gyral/http`, `@gyral/router`, `@gyral/time`, `@gyral/ssr`, `@gyral/testing` and
`@gyral/devtools` take `@gyral/core` as a peer dependency at their own exact version, so they
always use your app's copy of core: give every `@gyral/*` package the same version. Your
package manager reports a mismatch when it installs (pnpm lists the unmet peer, npm stops with
`ERESOLVE`), and a package that loads with another release of core throws
[G0016](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0016) in development, naming both versions.

## The Vite plugins

`gyral()` from `@gyral/core/vite` returns the Vite plugins every Gyral app needs. Put it in the
config's `plugins`, beside any plugins of your own (`plugins: [gyral(), mine()]`); its settings
come through the plugins themselves, so there is nothing to spread or merge:

```ts
// vite.config.ts
import { defineConfig } from 'vite';
import { gyral } from '@gyral/core/vite';

export default defineConfig({
  plugins: [gyral()],
});
```

- **The template compiler.** In `vite build` it checks every `html` and `svg` template,
  dependencies included, fails the build with a code frame on a rule violation, and replaces each
  template with a precompiled object, so the bundle doesn't carry the runtime template preparer.
  The dev server and Vitest keep the runtime path, which checks the same rules on first render;
  there a template-locations plugin tells the runtime where each template is written, so its
  errors and hydration mismatches name your file, line and column. With `parse5` installed, the
  build also compares each template with a full HTML parser's result.
- **Server code under `vite dev`.** Vite, not Node, loads `@gyral/*` (and your dependencies that
  use them) in server code, so server rendering there gets development output and shares one
  copy of `@gyral/core`.
- **Pre-bundling.** The dev server and Vitest pre-bundle the browser entry points of every
  Gyral package installed for the app, and of your direct dependencies that use Gyral (a design
  system, a widget library), all together, so they never load a second copy of `@gyral/core`
  partway through a run. `gyral()` also warns once when `@gyral/core` is installed more than once
  ([G0015](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0015)): pin one version with your package manager's overrides.
- **`optimize: 'auto'`** points Vite's startup scan at the modules that define components, and
  at a Vitest browser project's tests, so Vite finds everything they import before the first
  page or test loads instead of reloading partway through. It is on by default when Vite runs as
  a custom server (`appType: 'custom'`, as the [development server](https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/#development-server)
  does); set it yourself in a Vitest browser project. A list adds dependencies to pre-bundle,
  `gyral({ optimize: ['some-dep'] })`, and `optimize: false` turns the scan off.
- **`clientOnly: true`**, for apps no server renders, leaves the hydration code out of the
  browser bundle. See [Client-only builds](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/#client-only-builds).
- **`components: true`** loads each component's module once its tag is on the page, so pages
  need no client entry. See
  [Code splitting](https://gyral.dev/docs/code-splitting/#load-components-by-whats-on-the-page).
- **`types`**: `gyral()` writes [element typings](https://gyral.dev/docs/components/#anatomy-of-define) to
  `.gyral/elements.d.ts` by scanning `src`; `types: false` turns that off.

Import `html` from `@gyral/core` wherever you write templates. The compiler follows that import,
and refuses an alias (`const h = html`) it can't follow. For Vitest browser tests, add `gyral()`
to each browser project's config too ([Testing](https://gyral.dev/docs/testing/#browser-tests)).

`gyralVitePreset(options)` returns the same plugins as `{ plugins, optimizeDeps }`, for a config
that spreads it in. `npx @gyral/codemod 0.3.8` rewrites such a config to `plugins: [gyral()]`
where it can prove the result the same, and lists the configs it leaves.

## The ESLint plugin

`@gyral/core/eslint` shows the compiler's template errors in your editor, with the same
messages, checks that `each` rows read only their arguments, and finds intent parsers no
template names:

```js
// eslint.config.js
import gyral from '@gyral/core/eslint';

export default [{ files: ['src/**/*.ts'], ...gyral.configs.recommended }];
```

`recommended` turns on `gyral/template`, `gyral/each-row-purity` and `gyral/intent-event` (an
[`on()` parser](https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/#parsers-typed-by-their-event) bound to another event) as errors,
and `gyral/unused-intent` and `gyral/prefer-built-in` as warnings. `gyral/prefer-built-in` finds
hand-written versions of what Gyral has built in and names the built-in: a dialog opened with
`showModal()` (`?modal`), `.focus()` in a driver (the `focus()` command), `JSON.parse` of an
attribute or prop (`prop.json()`), a subscription that drops repeated values by hand (`equals`),
a record of drivers outside tests (a list), and a parser that checks the event's type, modifier
keys, `Number(value)` of a number input or `composedPath()[0]` (`on()`). It works without Vite.
See [Views](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#checked-before-it-runs) for what the template rules catch.

## Publishing a component library

A package of Gyral components, such as a design system or a set of widgets, must share the
app's copy of `@gyral/core`: a stylesheet from `css` or a store made by another copy doesn't work
in the app's. List core as a peer dependency with a caret range, and as a dev dependency at the
version you develop against:

```json
{
  "peerDependencies": { "@gyral/core": "^0.3.8" },
  "devDependencies": { "@gyral/core": "0.3.8" }
}
```

- **A peer, never a dependency.** A dependency pinned to one version installs a second core
  whenever the app has another one ([G0015](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0015)); a peer uses the app's.
- **A caret range**: `^0.3.8` is 0.3.8 up to, but not including, 0.4.0. Its lower bound is the
  oldest core you test against. Gyral's own packages pin core exactly because they use its
  internals; a library uses the public API, so any core in the range works. Other Gyral packages
  the library imports, such as `@gyral/http`, are caret peers too.
- **Public entry points only**: `@gyral/core`, `@gyral/core/storage` and the other documented
  entries, never `@gyral/core/internal` or a file path, which change in any release. Import
  `html`, `svg` and `css` from `@gyral/core` itself where you write templates, so the app's
  template compiler sees them.
- **Templates as written.** Publish ES modules with their `html` templates as they are. The
  app's build compiles every template it bundles, `node_modules` included, and reads every
  installed package that lists `@gyral/core`, as a peer too, for the features its components
  use ([what the build reads](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/#what-the-build-reads)).
- **Test against the range**: run the library's tests with the lowest core its range allows and
  with the newest. `npx @gyral/mcp@0.3.8 skill --check` in its CI keeps the
  [agent skill](https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/#the-agent-skill) it carries on the version it develops
  against.

## What's inside

`@gyral/core` has no runtime dependencies. Its view layer was written for Gyral alone, from the
platform's own primitives: `<template>` cloning, constructable stylesheets, Declarative Shadow
DOM. Commands run on a small built-in runtime (one `AbortController` per task) that handles
cancellation, concurrency lanes and retries.

Apps ship only the features they use. `each`, `raw`, hooks, commands, stores and the prop builders
register themselves when your code first calls them, so an app that never calls one doesn't
bundle it, and the hydration code is a separate chunk that only server-rendered pages fetch.
Measured on Gyral's examples at 0.3.8 (KiB gzip, production builds with `gyral()`):

| App                      | First load | All chunks |
| ------------------------ | ---------- | ---------- |
| hello-world              | 9.7        | 12.1       |
| hello-world, client-only | 8.6        | 8.6        |
| isomorphic (SSR)         | 15.6       | 18.6       |
| no-js-first (SSR, forms) | 20.0       | 20.1       |

"First load" is the entry chunk and what it imports statically: what a page downloads before any
lazy `import()`. The no-js-first example loads its components
[by what's on the page](https://gyral.dev/docs/code-splitting/#load-components-by-whats-on-the-page), so its first
load counts what a page with every component preloads, the hydration chunk included. Builds leave
out view transitions, the frame lane and custom states unless a module names their spec field (the
build reads your code and the packages that depend on Gyral; see [what the build
reads](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/#what-the-build-reads)), `on()` is bundled only by apps that call it,
and production builds print short
[error codes](https://gyral.dev/errors/) instead of messages. [Error handling](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/), which every
app carries, costs about 0.75 KiB. The client-only row is the same app built with
[`clientOnly: true`](https://gyral.dev/docs/rendering-modes/#client-only-builds). The isomorphic example
routes, and the router's [scroll and focus handling](https://gyral.dev/docs/routing/#scroll-and-focus) costs it
about 0.5 KiB of first load; the History API code (about 0.75 KiB) loads only in browsers without
the Navigation API.

Browser code targets [Baseline](https://web.dev/baseline) "widely available" features. Newer
APIs, such as the Navigation API, URLPattern, invoker commands and View Transitions, are
feature-detected and used as enhancements.

## Known issues

- **Some markup isn't handled yet by the template checks**: `<select>` content under the new
  customizable-select parsing, CDATA in SVG, and `<noscript>` as raw text. Keep these out of
  templates, or put them in `raw()` on the server.
- **Deno and Cloudflare Workers have only had a spot check** for server rendering: a
  `renderPage` bundle ran on Deno and in a local Workers runtime, but adapters, deployed edge
  behavior, bindings and assets aren't tested (see
  [Deploying](https://gyral.dev/docs/deploying/#bun-deno-and-cloudflare-workers)).
- **Without a preload hint, the hydration chunk loads one round trip after the entry** on
  server-rendered pages. Pass `clientAssetsFromManifest()`'s `modulepreload` to `renderPage` (see
  [Static sites](https://gyral.dev/docs/static-sites/#a-static-build)); `productionServer` hands it to your app,
  with an `assets(modules)` that adds a page's lazily imported route chunks.

---

# API reference

> The public API of every Gyral package, generated from the type declarations at build time so it always matches the code.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/api/

Each package's page lists everything it exports, entry point by entry point: the declaration as
written in the source (function bodies left out) and its documentation comment. The pages are
generated from the packages this site is built with, every time it's built, so they can't drift
from the code.

> **Writing code? Start from working code, not from the reference.** [Recipes](https://gyral.dev/docs/recipes/)
> has a task list with filters and a signup form, with their tests, and [Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/)
> opens with a complete validated form. Adapt the closest one and check it; come here to look up
> a name an example or a compiler error shows you. Most of the types are inferred, so you rarely
> write them yourself.

| Package                                  | What's in it                                                                   |
| ---------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| [`@gyral/core`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/core/)         | `define`, commands, subscriptions, stores, forms, the view layer; Vite, ESLint |
| [`@gyral/http`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/http/)         | `get`, `request`, `submitForm`, the `http` driver; `fakeHttp` for tests        |
| [`@gyral/router`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/router/)     | `routes`, `listen`, `navigate`, `setHead`, `makeRouter`                        |
| [`@gyral/time`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/time/)         | `delay`, `debounce`, `every`                                                   |
| [`@gyral/ssr`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/ssr/)           | `renderPage`, `formAction`, CSP; static generation, Node adapter, dev server   |
| [`@gyral/testing`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/testing/)   | `step`, `run`, `mount`, `parse`, fake drivers, virtual time, `mountSsr`        |
| [`@gyral/devtools`](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/devtools/) | `mountDevtools` and the panel                                                  |

`@gyral/mcp` (an MCP server for coding agents) and `create-gyral` (the app scaffolder) aren't
in this reference; [Packages](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/) describes them.

## Reading the reference

- **Types are the contract.** A component is `define<State, Msg, Props, Output>()(tag, spec)`;
  `ComponentSpec` in `@gyral/core` describes every field of `spec`.
- **Helper types are exported.** `Reducer`, `Variant`, `ParseResult` and `StandardSchemaV1`
  (type-only) are the types `Update`, `IntentParser` and the form helpers are
  built from, so a reducer or parser written outside a spec can be typed without copying
  Gyral's definitions.
- **Functions return data.** Command helpers such as `get`, `delay` and `navigate` return a
  `Command`, which does nothing until a reducer returns it.
- **The view layer is Gyral's own.** `html`, `css`, `each`, `keyed`, `raw`, `defineHook` and
  `nothing` are documented with the rest of `@gyral/core`; `@gyral/core/vite` is `gyral()`, the Vite
  plugins, and `@gyral/core/eslint` the lint rules. Server rendering is `@gyral/ssr`.

The guides explain how the pieces fit together: start with [Components](https://gyral.dev/docs/components/).

---

# Browser support

> Gyral targets Baseline widely available browser features, with explicit fallbacks and progressive enhancement for newer platform APIs.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/browser-support/

Shipped browser code targets **Baseline widely available**: features supported across the
major browser engines for at least 30 months. The repository uses the Browserslist query
`baseline widely available`; compatibility lint checks JavaScript and CSS. This is a moving
feature floor, not a promise to support one permanently fixed browser version.

Custom elements, Shadow DOM, template cloning, constructable stylesheets and declarative
shadow roots are part of that floor. Gyral renders with these native primitives. On the server
and in builds, Gyral supports both Node LTS lines, 24 and 26, and its gate runs on each;
`create-gyral` and `@gyral/mcp` also run on Node 22.12 and later, and `@gyral/codemod` on 22.18
or later and 24.11 or later. Browser support and server-runtime support are separate questions.

## What happens without newer APIs

| Native enhancement      | Baseline behavior                                                                       |
| ----------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `URLPattern`            | A constrained literal/parameter matcher with the same supported patterns                |
| Navigation API          | Lazy History API implementation, popstate and link capture                              |
| `command`/`commandfor`  | Lazy component-scoped command shim                                                      |
| `moveBefore()`          | `insertBefore()`; test focus-sensitive moves in your app                                |
| `requestIdleCallback()` | A short timer releases the island                                                       |
| `startViewTransition()` | Ordinary rendering; reduced motion also skips the transition                            |
| `:state()`              | State enhancement is skipped; keep meaning in markup and ARIA                           |
| Popover API             | Model-driven toggling is skipped; provide an accessible inline alternative where needed |
| The `gyral` HTML policy | Ordinary string parsing when the API is absent                                          |

Gyral never installs a global browser polyfill. Substantial fallbacks are internal modules
loaded when needed; small fallbacks stay beside the native call. Capability checks for Node
or workers, such as the absence of animation frames, remain even as browser support improves.

## Removal dates

These dates follow the `web-features` 3.35.0 snapshot in
[ADR 0003](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/v0.3.8/docs/design-docs/0003-browser-baseline.md),
adding 30 months to newly available. They are scheduled review points, not claims that the
fallback has already been removed:

| Primitive                 | Widely available date |
| ------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `Promise.withResolvers()` | 2026-09-05            |
| `AbortSignal.any()`       | 2026-09-19            |
| `AbortSignal.timeout()`   | 2026-10-18            |
| Custom states             | 2026-11-17            |
| Popover                   | 2027-07-27            |
| `URLPattern`              | 2028-03-15            |
| View Transitions          | 2028-04-14            |
| Invoker commands          | 2028-06-12            |
| Navigation API            | 2028-07-13            |
| Trusted Types             | 2028-08-24            |

`moveBefore()` and `requestIdleCallback()` have no Baseline removal date in that snapshot.
The [native-first audit](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/v0.3.8/docs/references/native-first-audit-2026-10-11.md)
records why cancellable and virtual-time timers remain useful even when native timeout
signals become widely available.

## Your application's features

Feature-detect newer JavaScript APIs and keep a working experience when they are absent.
Guard newer CSS with `@supports`, preserving an accessible baseline layout. Do not make
essential labels, errors or interactions depend on a skipped enhancement. Check current
[Baseline data](https://web.dev/baseline) before choosing a new primitive, and test your actual
minimum browser versions.

SSR mounting in `@gyral/testing` uses `setHTMLUnsafe()` to reproduce declarative shadow roots,
so choose a test browser that supports it. The repository runs real Chromium tests in
development and production configurations. Those tests are not evidence that every app flow
has also been tested in Firefox or Safari.

---

# Versioning and stability

> Understand Gyral's 0.x API policy, package versions, how to upgrade and which entry points are internal.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/versioning/

Gyral is in **0.x**. A minor version can include breaking changes. Read its upgrade guide
and the package changelogs before moving to it; do not treat every 0.x minor as an
interchangeable dependency update.

## Public and internal APIs

Use documented public package entries. Entries containing `/internal` are for Gyral's own
packages and have no stability promise. A symbol being technically exported does not make
an internal entry an application API. The
[export inventory](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/v0.3.8/docs/references/public-api-0.3.1.md)
records the public boundary of 0.3.8: every entry and what it exports.

The `@gyral/*` packages and `create-gyral` release together at a shared version: keep every
`@gyral/*` package your app installs on that one version. Gyral's packages take `@gyral/core` as a
peer at their exact version, so your package manager reports a mismatch when it installs (pnpm
lists the unmet peer, npm stops with `ERESOLVE`), and a package that loads with another release
of core throws [G0016](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0016) in development. The
[package guide](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#one-version-of-every-package) explains what each app needs.

## Releases

These guides describe **0.3.8**, the `latest` version on npm. Every package is published
from GitHub Actions with npm provenance; install from the registry. Today npm has releases
only, under the `latest` tag.

For a released application, pin the registry version you verified and retain the lockfile.
Deploy server output and client assets from the same build: stale HTML with new component
templates can cause hydration mismatches. Versioned hashed assets help keep that agreement.

Breaking changes wait for a new minor version, and that release gets an upgrade guide in these
docs. On an older 0.3.x release? Install 0.3.8 and read the
[core changelog](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/main/packages/core/CHANGELOG.md).

## Upgrade with evidence

1. Read the changelogs for every release between yours and the target, and the upgrade guide
   when the target is a new minor version.
2. Update packages together and install from the lockfile.
3. Commit, then run `npx @gyral/codemod 0.3.8` from the app's directory. It moves code to
   0.3.8's APIs wherever it can prove the rewrite safe: a spread-in `gyralVitePreset()` becomes
   `plugins: [gyral()]`,
   driver records outside tests become [lists](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/#substituting-drivers), and
   `subscription('feed', …)` becomes `subscription(feed, …)` where the module declares the
   `feed` token. It lists every candidate it leaves, with `file:line` and the reason, and only
   writes into a clean git working tree (`--dry` prints the diff instead), so `git diff` shows
   what it did.
4. Run ESLint with `gyral.configs.recommended` from `@gyral/core/eslint`. `gyral/prefer-built-in`
   names code that a built-in replaces, such as a parser that checks modifier keys by hand
   (`on()`), and `gyral/intent-event` an `on()` parser bound to another event
   ([the rules](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#the-eslint-plugin)).
5. Run typechecking, component/browser tests and the production build. In development, a view
   that reads something besides its state, props and stores warns ([G0017](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0017)),
   because Gyral skips renders whose inputs are unchanged.
6. Test server/client hydration, edited forms, routing and the production CSP if your app
   uses them. Check payload size for the pages whose loading matters.
7. Update the agent skill your project carries:
   `npx @gyral/mcp@0.3.8 skill` ([coding agents](https://gyral.dev/docs/coding-agents/#the-agent-skill)).

The generated [API reference](https://gyral.dev/docs/api/) describes the packages installed for this site's
build. Consult the changelog for the exact version your app runs:
[core](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/main/packages/core/CHANGELOG.md),
[HTTP](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/main/packages/http/CHANGELOG.md),
[router](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/main/packages/router/CHANGELOG.md),
[SSR](https://github.com/gyraljs/gyral/blob/main/packages/ssr/CHANGELOG.md) and the other package
directories. Report a regression with the versions, a small reproducer and the expected
behavior. The repository's `pnpm check` is its release-quality gate.

---

# Error codes

> Every code a production build of Gyral prints, such as G0010: what the message says, what it means and how to fix it.

Source: https://gyral.dev/errors/

Development builds of `@gyral/core` print each diagnostic in full. Production builds print a short line instead, so the message texts stay out of your bundle: `Gyral`, the code, the message’s arguments in order, and a link to this page.

```text
Gyral G0010 my-cart Add https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0010
```

Read that one as: `<my-cart>` has no update for the message `Add`. Find the code below; its message shows where each argument goes. For the full sentence, reproduce the problem in development (the dev server, tests, or a build with `--mode development`). A hydration mismatch keeps its own sentence in production and ends with its code and link.

The codes and messages are read from `@gyral/core` 0.3.8, the version this site is built with; codes are never reused.

## Components

### G0001

```text
<{tag}> is a browser element (render it on the server with @gyral/ssr).
```

Arguments: `tag`.

Outside the browser, `define()` only records your component for the server renderer, so there is no element class to construct: `new MyElement()` on the server throws this.

**Fix:** Render the component on the server through `@gyral/ssr` (`renderPage`, `renderToString`), instead of constructing it.

### G0010

```text
<{tag}> has no update for message "{message}".
```

Arguments: `tag`, `message`.

A component received a message whose `_tag` has no reducer in its `update`, so the message was dropped. It is usually a typo, or a reducer you forgot.

**Fix:** Add a reducer for the message to the component’s `update`, or stop sending it.

### G0011

```text
<{tag}> has no intent parser for data-intent="{intent}".
```

Arguments: `tag`, `intent`.

An event reached an element whose `data-intent` names an intent the component has no parser for, so the user’s action was ignored.

**Fix:** Add a parser with that name to the spec’s `intent`, or correct the name in the view (`data-intent=${i.Name}` catches typos at compile time).

### G0012

```text
<{tag}> intent parser for "{intent}" failed
```

Arguments: `tag`, `intent`.

An asynchronous intent parser rejected. The error is logged with this message, and the event produced no message.

**Fix:** Handle failures inside the parser (return a message that describes the failure, or `undefined`), or move the fallible work into a command with `onFailure`.

### G0013

```text
<{tag}> focus("{selector}") matched no focusable element.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `selector`.

A `focus(selector)` command found no element to focus in the component’s root after the render, so focus stayed where it was. Keyboard and screen reader users notice.

**Fix:** Make the selector match an element inside the component (its shadow root, or its children for `shadow: false`). Give targets that aren’t focusable, such as headings, `tabindex="-1"`.

### G0014

```text
<{tag}> is on the page, but no custom element named "{tag}" is defined {seconds} s after it loaded, so it renders nothing. If it is one of your components, import the module that calls define()('{tag}', …) from the entry; for a third-party element, load its package. Ignore this for an element defined later on purpose.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `seconds`.

Development builds look for custom-element tags on the page that nothing has defined, 3 seconds after load and again after each later `define()`. Such an element renders nothing: usually the entry never imports the module that defines it.

**Fix:** Import the component’s module from the entry (or from a module the entry imports). For a third-party element, load its package; ignore the warning for an element you define later on purpose.

### G0015

```text
Two copies of @gyral/core run in this page: {first} from {firstUrl}, and {second} from {secondUrl}. A value one copy makes, such as a stylesheet from css or a store, does not work in the other. Install one copy: pin @gyral/core to one version with your package manager's overrides (gyral() warns when it is installed more than once).
```

Arguments: `first`, `firstUrl`, `second`, `secondUrl`.

Development only: two copies of `@gyral/core` run in the page. A value one copy makes, such as a stylesheet from `css` or a store, doesn’t work in the other, so components fail far from the cause (`styles.flatMap is not a function`). `gyral()` also warns at startup, in dev and builds, when the package is installed more than once, naming each copy’s version, folder and the packages that use it.

**Fix:** Give every `@gyral/*` package the same version: they take `@gyral/core` as a peer, so they share the app’s copy. For a library that pins another core, pin `@gyral/core` to one version with your package manager’s overrides (pnpm or npm `overrides`, Yarn `resolutions`) and reinstall. A library lists `@gyral/core` as a peer dependency ([Publishing a component library](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#publishing-a-component-library)).

### G0016

```text
{package} {version} needs @gyral/core {version}, but this app has @gyral/core {core}. Gyral's packages are released together: install the same version of every @gyral package.
```

Arguments: `package`, `version`, `core`.

A Gyral package (`@gyral/http`, `router`, `time`, `ssr`, `testing` or `devtools`) loaded with a `@gyral/core` of another release. Each one uses core’s internals, which change between releases, so it checks core’s version when it loads. They take `@gyral/core` as a peer at their exact version, so the package manager normally reports the mismatch when it installs: pnpm lists the unmet peer, npm stops with `ERESOLVE`. Development throws, naming both versions; production logs this warning and carries on.

**Fix:** Install the same version of every `@gyral/*` package the app uses, and check that the lockfile resolves one version of each ([One version of every package](https://gyral.dev/docs/packages/#one-version-of-every-package)).

### G0017

```text
<{tag}> rendered differently with the same state, props and stores, so its view reads something else, such as Date.now(), a module variable or the DOM. A component renders only when one of them changes (0.3.8): move what the view reads into state, a prop or a store.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

Development only: a component renders only when its state, a declared prop or a declared store’s value changes, and this one rendered differently when Gyral rendered a skipped view again to check it. So its view reads something else, such as `Date.now()`, `Math.random()`, a module variable or the DOM, and on the page it shows a stale value until one of its inputs changes. Development checks up to 50 skipped views per render pass (a different 50 each pass when more are skipped, so every component is checked within a few passes) and warns once per component.

**Fix:** Move what the view reads into state (the time from an `every` subscription, a random value from a command), a prop or a store, so that a change to it renders the component ([Pure means repeatable](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#pure-means-repeatable)).

### G0018

```text
The parser of intent "{intent}" is on("{expected}"), but a "{actual}" event reached it. Bind the intent to that event (data-intent-{expected}=${…}), or give it a parser of its own.
```

Arguments: `intent`, `expected`, `actual`.

The intent’s parser is `on(event, …)`, written for one event type, but another event reached it: the template binds the intent to a different event, through the element’s own trigger, `data-intent-on` or another `data-intent-<event>` attribute. Development throws; production declines the event, as a parser that returns `undefined` does. The `gyral/intent-event` ESLint rule reports the same binding in the editor.

**Fix:** Bind the intent to the parser’s event, `data-intent-keydown=${i.Move}` for `on("keydown", …)`, or give the other event an intent and a parser of its own ([Parsers typed by their event](https://gyral.dev/docs/intent/#parsers-typed-by-their-event)).

## Props

### G0020

```text
<{tag}> prop "{prop}" has an asynchronous schema; it must be synchronous.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `prop`.

A prop’s Standard Schema returned a promise. Props are validated synchronously, while the element updates and renders, so they can’t wait for it.

**Fix:** Use a synchronous schema or a type guard for the prop, and do asynchronous checks in a command.

### G0021

```text
<{tag}> prop "{prop}" got an invalid value from {source}, so it is treated as missing: {issues}
```

Arguments: `tag`, `prop`, `source`, `issues`.

A prop value failed its type or its schema, so it is treated as missing and its `default` applies. Attributes are checked in every build; property sets and hydration seeds in development only.

**Fix:** Pass a value that matches the prop’s declaration (a numeric string for `prop.number`, valid JSON for `prop.json`), or loosen the schema.

### G0022

```text
<{tag}> is missing required prop(s): {props}.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `props`.

A component rendered for the first time while props declared `required` were still missing. The parent probably forgot an attribute or a property.

**Fix:** Set the prop on the element (an attribute, or `.prop=${…}`) before it renders, or give it a `default` instead of `required`.

### G0023

```text
<{tag}> declares prop(s) named like a member every element already has: {props}. The prop would replace it: a prop named "hidden" hides the element, one named "state" hides the component's model. Rename the property. The name of one of Gyral's members (state, send, drivers, stores) can stay the attribute: badge: prop.string({ attribute: "state" }).
```

Arguments: `tag`, `props`.

A component declares props named like a member every element already has: a built-in property (`hidden`, `title`, `id`), or one of Gyral’s (`state`, `send`, `drivers`, `stores`, `initialMessages`, the custom-element callbacks). The prop would replace the member: a prop named `hidden` hides the element, one named `state` hides the component’s model. TypeScript rejects these names and development throws; production warns about built-in names.

**Fix:** Rename the property. One of Gyral’s names can stay the public attribute: `badge: prop.string({ attribute: "state" })`.

### G0024

```text
<{tag}> has a "{attribute}" attribute, which no prop reads: HTML lowercases attribute names, and prop {prop} reads "{expected}". Write {expected}="…", or set the property (el.{prop} = …).
```

Arguments: `tag`, `attribute`, `prop`, `expected`.

Development only: the element carries an attribute HTML lowercased from a camelCase prop’s name, such as `playerbase` for `playerBase`, written in the page’s HTML or set by a host framework. The prop reads its kebab-case attribute, `player-base`, so the value never reached it.

**Fix:** Write the prop’s attribute (`player-base="…"`), or set the property in code. In templates, the build and ESLint report the same mistake ([template rules](https://gyral.dev/docs/views/#checked-before-it-runs)).

## Scheduling

### G0030

```text
gyral: a deferred callback failed
```

Arguments: none.

A callback Gyral deferred to a microtask threw: delivering a child component’s output to its parent. The parent may not have received the output.

**Fix:** Look at the error logged with this message, and make sure the parent’s `child()` mapper and any `gyral-output` listener don’t throw.

### G0031

```text
<{tag}> view failed; it shows its error view, or its previous DOM stays.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

A component’s `view` threw during a render. Gyral reports a `GyralError` (phase `view`) through its error channel and keeps rendering the other components. The component renders its `error` view if its spec has one; otherwise its DOM shows its previous state.

**Fix:** Fix the exception in the view, using the `cause` of the reported error. It is often a field read on state that has a different shape than the view expects. Give the spec an `error(failure, state)` view so users see a fallback ([Error handling](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/)).

### G0032

```text
gyral: post-render work failed
```

Arguments: none.

Work that runs after a render failed: a focus command, custom states from `states`, the `Hydrated` message, or the commands `init` returned for a resumed component.

**Fix:** Fix the exception logged with this message, typically in the spec’s `states` function or the `Hydrated` reducer.

### G0033

```text
gyral: rendering did not settle in one flush (a cycle between {tags}). Components are probably feeding each other props or messages; break the cycle with a condition in update.
```

Arguments: `tags`.

Rendering didn’t settle in one flush: the named components kept re-rendering each other. Components are probably feeding each other props or messages in a cycle. Development throws; production logs it and drops the rest of the work so the page doesn’t freeze.

**Fix:** Break the cycle with a condition in `update`, for example by sending a message or changing state only when the value actually differs.

### G0034

```text
settled(): the page did not settle after {rounds} flushes or busy turns. A stream is emitting without pause, or components (or drivers) are feeding each other messages in a cycle.
```

Arguments: `rounds`.

`settled()` rejected because messages kept arriving: more than the given number of flushes or busy turns went by without a quiet moment. Something is sending messages in a cycle, or a stream emits on every turn.

**Fix:** Find the cycle and break it with a condition in `update`, or substitute the chatty driver in the test.

## Commands

### G0040

```text
{owner}: the onSuccess or onFailure mapper for driver "{driver}" threw; no message was sent.
```

Arguments: `owner`, `driver`.

A command’s `onSuccess` or `onFailure` mapper threw while turning a driver’s result into a message, so the result never reached `update`. It is reported as a `GyralError` (phase `command`), and the component’s `Errored` reducer, if any, receives it.

**Fix:** Make the mapper total: return a message, or `undefined`, for every input.

### G0041

```text
{owner}: driver "{driver}" failed and the command has no onFailure.
```

Arguments: `owner`, `driver`.

A driver failed, after any `retry()` policy, and the command has no `onFailure`. This is an error, not a warning: it is reported as a `GyralError` (phase `command`) and reaches the component’s `Errored` reducer, if any. Without one, the component can’t react: a spinner may spin forever.

**Fix:** Give the command an `onFailure` that turns the error into a message, and handle that message in `update`. Expected failures (the network, a 5xx, a refusal) should always be messages.

### G0042

```text
gyral: subscription "{name}" failed to unsubscribe
```

Arguments: `name`.

The function (or `unsubscribe()`) a `subscription()` returned threw when Gyral released the source, so the source may still be sending values or holding listeners.

**Fix:** Make the stop function that `subscribe` returns safe to call once, and return a function or an object with `unsubscribe()`.

### G0043

```text
{owner}: no driver provides "{driver}". It is a driver token: provide its implementation with provideDrivers(root, [token.provide(run)]) or el.drivers. A page provides it before its components' first render: before importing them, or later in the same task (no await in between).
```

Arguments: `owner`, `driver`.

The command’s driver is a token: `defineDriver<I, O, E>(name)` without an implementation of its own. Nothing above the component provides that name, so the command can’t run. It is reported through the error channel (phase `command`); `onFailure` isn’t called, because there was no driver to fail.

**Fix:** Provide the driver where the app starts, `provideDrivers(document.body, [token.provide(run)])`, or on the element with `el.drivers`. A page provides it before its components first render: before importing them, or later in the same task with no `await` in between ([Substituting drivers](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/#substituting-drivers)). In tests, pass a fake of the token, `fakeDriver(token)`, which takes its name ([Drivers the app provides](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/#drivers-the-app-provides)).

### G0044

```text
Two drivers named "{name}" in one list of drivers: give each a name of its own, or drop one.
```

Arguments: `name`.

Development only: a list of drivers (for `provideDrivers`, `el.drivers`, `<gyral-drivers>`, `mount({ drivers })` or a store) has two drivers with the same name. A command finds its driver by name, so only one of them could ever run. Development throws; production has no check and uses the first.

**Fix:** Drop one of them, or give each driver a name of its own and build each command from the driver it should use.

### G0045

```text
A driver supplied as "{key}" is named "{name}", so commands of the "{name}" driver never use it. Supply drivers as a list, each under its own name (provideDrivers(root, [driver])), or make the key match.
```

Arguments: `key`, `name`.

Development only: a record of drivers has a key that isn’t the name of the driver under it, such as `{ api: makeHttpDriver() }` for a driver named `http`. A command looks its driver up by the driver’s own name, `http` here, so that entry is never used: the lookup goes on to the next provider and, last, to the command’s own driver (for a token, [G0043](https://gyral.dev/errors/#G0043)). Development warns once per record.

**Fix:** Supply the drivers as a list, each under its own name, `provideDrivers(root, [makeHttpDriver()])`, or make the key the driver’s name ([Substituting drivers](https://gyral.dev/docs/effects/#substituting-drivers)).

## Stores

### G0050

```text
<{tag}> uses store "{store}" without declaring it. Add it to the spec: stores: [{store}], so the component subscribes to its changes.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `store`.

A component read a store with `ctx.read(store)`, or sent to one, without listing it in its spec. A component subscribes only to the stores it declares, so it would miss the store’s changes.

**Fix:** Declare the store in the spec, for example `stores: [cart]`.

### G0051

```text
store "{store}": the server's seed failed its schema, so it starts from init. Issues: {issues}
```

Arguments: `store`, `issues`.

The store state the server seeded into the page failed the store’s `schema`, so the browser discarded it and the store starts from `init`. The page may show different data than the server rendered.

**Fix:** Fix the state the server sends, or align the store’s `schema` with it.

### G0052

```text
unreadable {attribute} seed on {where}
```

Arguments: `attribute`, `where`.

The store seed on the page, or on a `<gyral-stores>` provider, isn’t valid JSON, so every store in it starts from `init`.

**Fix:** Let `@gyral/ssr` write the seed (`renderPage({ stores })`, or the provider’s `.instances`) instead of writing it by hand, and check that nothing rewrites or truncates the HTML on its way.

### G0053

```text
<{tag}> reads store "{store}" during a server render without a store scope. Pass the request's store instances to renderPage({ stores }) or renderToString(value, { stores }).
```

Arguments: `tag`, `store`.

A component read a store during a server render without a store scope. On the server each request needs its own store instances, and without a scope Gyral can’t tell whose state to read.

**Fix:** Render through `@gyral/ssr` and pass the request’s instances: `renderPage({ stores })` or `renderToString(value, { stores })`.

### G0054

```text
store "{store}" sends to "{target}" but is not held by a store scope (a registry, <gyral-stores> or the page default), so the message is dropped.
```

Arguments: `store`, `target`.

A store’s `update` sent a message to another store, but this store instance isn’t held by a store scope, so the message has nowhere to go and is dropped.

**Fix:** Let a scope hold the instance: the page’s default, a `<gyral-stores>` provider (`.instances=${[…]}`), or a store registry in tests.

### G0055

```text
store "{store}" has no update for message "{message}".
```

Arguments: `store`, `message`.

A store received a message whose `_tag` has no reducer in its `update`, so the message was dropped and the change you expected didn’t happen.

**Fix:** Add a reducer for the message to the store’s `update`, or correct the tag being sent.

## Hydration

### G0060

```text
<{tag}> has an unreadable {attribute}
```

Arguments: `tag`, `attribute`.

A server-rendered component’s `data-gyral-seed` isn’t valid JSON, so the browser can’t resume the server’s state: the component starts from `init`, and its first render may not match the server’s HTML.

**Fix:** Don’t edit or write `data-gyral-seed` yourself. Look for whatever changes the server’s HTML on its way: a proxy, an HTML minifier, string templating.

### G0061

```text
gyral: hydration code failed to load; rendering fresh
```

Arguments: none.

The hydration code, which loads lazily with the first server-rendered component, failed to load, so server-rendered components render fresh instead of hydrating. The page works, but redoes the server’s work. It is usually a stale deploy: a cached page that points at a chunk that no longer exists.

**Fix:** Keep the previous build’s assets online for a while after a deploy, or don’t cache HTML that points at removed chunks. The network error is logged with this message.

### G0062

```text
gyral: hydration mismatch in {host} at {path}: expected {expected}, found {found}. The server's HTML differs from the first client render: a view that isn't deterministic (Date.now(), locale), a third party that changed the DOM before scripts ran, or a stale cached page (https://gyral.dev/docs/server-rendering/#mismatches).
```

Arguments: `host`, `path`, `expected`, `found`.

The server’s HTML differs from the first client render, so the component can’t be hydrated in place. Development throws `HydrationMismatch`, naming the template’s file and line; production keeps the sentence (the component, the DOM path, what was expected and found), ends it with this code, and renders the component fresh (G0063).

**Fix:** Make the view render the same on both sides: no `Date.now()`, random numbers or locale-dependent formatting in `view` (put them in state through a command). Also rule out a browser extension or script that changed the DOM before hydration, and a stale cached page.

### G0063

```text
<{tag}> was rendered fresh after a hydration mismatch:
```

Arguments: `tag`.

Production only: after a hydration mismatch (G0062, which follows in the same warning), Gyral cleared this component and rendered it fresh. The rest of the page stays hydrated, but this component flashes and redoes the server’s work.

**Fix:** Fix the mismatch the warning describes; reproducing it in development gives the full message and the template’s location.

## Templates

### G0069

```text
<{element}> ?{binding} does nothing: this build left the dialog and popover code out, because no module the build scanned binds it (a package that does not depend on Gyral is not scanned).
```

Arguments: `element`, `binding`.

Production only: a `?modal` or `?popover-open` binding ran in a build that left the dialog and popover code out, so the dialog didn’t open. The build adds that code when a module it reads binds one, in source or in a package’s compiled templates, and it doesn’t read installed packages that don’t depend on Gyral.

**Fix:** Make the package that ships the template depend on `@gyral/core` (a library lists it as a peer dependency), so the build reads it, or move the template into your own source.

### G0070

```text
gyral: an html template was not compiled: `{start}`. Under the gyral-compiled condition every html`…` must be compiled by the Gyral Vite preset.
```

Arguments: `start`.

A bundle built with the Vite preset leaves out the runtime template preparer, so every `html` template must be precompiled, and this one wasn’t. The build normally fails before this can happen.

**Fix:** Import `html` (and `svg`) from `@gyral/core`, or from a package listed in the compiler’s `sources`, and use it directly as a tag: the compiler can’t follow an alias, a call or a re-export.

### G0071

```text
gyral: template rule 11: a page shell rendered in the browser.
```

Arguments: none.

A page shell, a template with `<!doctype>`, `<html>`, `<head>` or `<body>`, was rendered in the browser. Only the server renders document-level tags. Development reports it as template rule 11, with the full explanation.

**Fix:** Render the page shell on the server with `@gyral/ssr`’s `renderPage`, and render only components in the browser.

### G0072

```text
gyral: this page's Trusted Types policy list does not allow the policy "gyral", so templates are parsed from plain strings, which works only while Trusted Types are not enforced. Add `trusted-types gyral` to the Content-Security-Policy.
```

Arguments: none.

Gyral parses template HTML and `raw()` markup through a Trusted Types policy named `gyral`. The page’s Content-Security-Policy has a `trusted-types` directive that lists allowed policy names without `gyral`, so the browser refused to create it. Gyral falls back to plain strings, which works only while the page doesn’t enforce Trusted Types (`require-trusted-types-for 'script'`). Development warns once.

**Fix:** Add `gyral` to the policy list: `trusted-types gyral` (with your own policies, if any). If you don’t use Trusted Types, remove the `trusted-types` directive.

## Error handling

### G0073

```text
<{tag}> update for "{message}" failed; the state is unchanged.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `message`.

A reducer threw while handling the named message. Nothing changed: the state stays as it was and the commands that reducer would have returned don’t run. It is reported as a `GyralError` (phase `update`), and the component’s `Errored` reducer, if any, receives it.

**Fix:** Fix the exception in that reducer, using the `cause` of the reported error. Add an `Errored` reducer if the component should show an error state ([Error handling](https://gyral.dev/docs/error-handling/)).

### G0074

```text
<{tag}> init failed; it shows its error view, or stays empty.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

A component’s `init` threw, so it has no state. It renders its `error(failure, undefined)` view if its spec has one, or stays empty. The error is reported as a `GyralError` (phase `init`).

**Fix:** Fix the exception in `init`, using the `cause` of the reported error; often a prop or seed read with an unexpected shape. Give the spec an `error` view for a visible fallback.

### G0075

```text
<{tag}> element hook failed; the other hooks still ran.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

An element hook’s `client` function threw. Gyral reported it (phase `hook`) and still ran the other hooks of that render; the element itself is in the DOM.

**Fix:** Fix the exception in the hook, using the `cause` of the reported error.

### G0076

```text
store "{store}": update for "{message}" failed; the state is unchanged.
```

Arguments: `store`, `message`.

A store’s reducer threw while handling the named message. The store’s state is unchanged and its commands don’t run. The error is reported as a `GyralError` (phase `store`); the sender isn’t affected.

**Fix:** Fix the exception in that store reducer, using the `cause` of the reported error.

### G0077

```text
store "{store}": a subscriber failed; the other subscribers were still notified.
```

Arguments: `store`.

A component that reads the store threw while handling `StoreChanged`. The other subscribers were still notified and the store’s commands still ran.

**Fix:** Fix the exception in that component’s `StoreChanged` reducer (or the code it calls), using the `cause` of the reported error.

### G0078

```text
<{tag}> failed to render on the server; it renders its error view (or nothing) and starts fresh in the browser.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

A component’s `init` or view threw during server rendering. It rendered its `error` view (or nothing), marked `data-gyral-error` and without a seed, and the rest of the page was sent; the browser starts that component fresh. `renderPage`’s `onError` received the error.

**Fix:** Fix the exception, using the error your `onError` received. Pass `onError: 'throw'` to `renderPage` if a failing component should fail the whole page instead, so the route can answer with its error page.

## Subscriptions

### G0079

```text
<{tag}> subscriptions returned two commands for lane "{lane}"; only the first runs. Give each its own `key`.
```

Arguments: `tag`, `lane`.

The component’s `subscriptions` returned two commands in the same lane: the same `key`, or no key and the same driver. Gyral keeps one running command per lane, so only the first runs. Development warns.

**Fix:** Give each subscription its own `key`, such as one per room or per URL.

### G0080

```text
<{tag}> subscriptions kept restarting: a subscription's input data changes with every message it sends (for example a timestamp or a counter in the input). Keep inputs to what should restart it; functions are ignored, so to restart on a new selector, change the key.
```

Arguments: `tag`.

A subscription restarted again and again: its input changed with every message it sent, so each new state asked for a different input, which restarted it. Gyral stops after 100 rounds rather than loop.

**Fix:** Keep a subscription’s input to what should restart it (an id, a URL), not values that its own messages change, such as a counter or a timestamp.

## Element calls

### G0085

```text
<{tag}> call("{selector}", "{method}") failed
```

Arguments: `tag`, `selector`, `method`.

A `call(selector, method, …args)` command failed after the render: no element of the component matched the selector, the element has no such method, or the method threw or rejected. The reported error’s `cause` says which. It is reported through the error channel (phase `command`).

**Fix:** Check that the element is rendered when the command runs (return the command from the reducer whose new state renders it), that the selector matches inside the component’s own tree, and that the method exists on that element.

### G0086

```text
call("{selector}", "{method}"): arguments must be plain data.
```

Arguments: `selector`, `method`.

Development checks that a `call()` command’s arguments are plain data that can be cloned (strings, numbers, arrays and plain objects). A function, an element or a class instance would make the command impossible to compare or record in a test.

**Fix:** Pass plain data, and let the element look up anything else itself.

---

# @gyral/core

> Gyral core: Model-View-Intent web components on the web platform, with their own view layer.

Source: https://gyral.dev/docs/api/core/

Gyral core: Model-View-Intent web components on the web platform, with their own view layer.

```sh
npm install @gyral/core
```

> **Writing code? Start from working code, not from this page.** [Recipes](https://gyral.dev/docs/recipes/) has a task list with filters and a signup form, with their tests; [Forms](https://gyral.dev/docs/forms/) opens with a complete validated form; [Getting started](https://gyral.dev/docs/getting-started/) builds a first component. Adapt the closest example and check it, then look a name up here when you are about to call it.

Generated from the package's type declarations. Entry points: [`@gyral/core`](#gyralcore), [`@gyral/core/storage`](#gyralcorestorage), [`@gyral/core/indexeddb`](#gyralcoreindexeddb), [`@gyral/core/vite`](#gyralcorevite), [`@gyral/core/eslint`](#gyralcoreeslint).
